## P081: Novel 3D-printed mesh-brace for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: a retrospective cohort study

Samuel Schaible

1

, Jan Gewiess

1

, Yann Bieri

1

, Moritz Deml

1

1

University Hospital Bern, Inselspital, Department of Orthopaedic Surgery and Traumatology, Bern, Switzerland

Introduction: Effective bracing in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) requires optimal curve correction while maintaining patient comfort to ensure compliance. We introduced a novel 3D-printed brace using polyamide 12 (PA12), a lightweight and flexible material combined with a breathable printing design, as an opportunity to enhance both treatment efficacy and comfort. The custom PA12 brace is designed with a triangle mesh pattern that is optimized for flexibility and breathability, while still providing the structural support needed for curve correction. This study aims to evaluate the clinical efficacy of the novel brace in AIS patients. Material and Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 30 AIS patients (mean age: 16.1 years, range: 7.6–22.1 years) treated with the PA12 mesh-brace over a mean follow-up of 37.5 months (range: 8.5-90.8 months). The primary outcome was radiographic assessment of Cobb angles pre-brace, at 2 months in-brace, and at the last follow-up. Secondary outcomes included sagittal balance parameters such as thoracic kyphosis (TK) and lumbar lordosis (LL), while qualitative feedback on comfort and compliance was collected through structured questionnaires. Paired t-tests were used to compare outcomes within groups, and independent t-tests were applied for between-group comparisons. Results: For the entire cohort, the mean major Cobb angle decreased from 29.3° (SD: 9.8, range: 12.3°-55.2°) pre-brace to 16.7° (SD: 10.5, range: 6.4°-42.1°) at 2 months (p < 0.001), and to 22.5° (SD: 12.2, range: 6.4°-50.7°) at the last follow-up (p < 0.001). The no-surgery group (n = 23; 77%) showed a significant 50.8% reduction in the major Cobb angle at 2 months (mean pre-brace: 24.4°, SD: 6.27, range: 12.3°-38.6°), with a regression of 33.2% by the last follow-up (mean last: 16.0°, p < 0.001). The overall mean reduction from pre-brace was 34.5% (p < 0.001). Minor Cobb angles in this group showed a similar pattern, with a 47.2% decrease at 2 months and a 25.1% decrease from pre-brace to last follow-up (p < 0.01). The no-surgery group also showed a significant improvement in LL from pre-brace to 2 months (p < 0.01), while TK did not show significant changes (p > 0.05). In the surgery group (n = 7; 23%), the major Cobb angle initially improved by 42.7% at 2 months (mean pre-brace: 37.0°, SD: 10.83, range: 24.5°-55.2°), but regressed significantly by 139.2% at the last follow-up (mean last: 50.7°, p < 0.001). Minor Cobb angles followed a similar pattern, with a 68.8% regression by the last follow-up (p < 0.05). TK and LL did not show significant changes in the surgery group (p > 0.05). Between-group comparisons revealed significant differences in major Cobb angles both pre-brace and at last follow-up (p < 0.001). Qualitative feedback was positive, particularly on comfort, with no treatment terminations. Conclusion: The 3D-printed PA12 mesh-brace demonstrated significant sustained curve correction in AIS patients with similar treatment response as polyethylene braces. The innovative design, lightweight material, and breathability contributed to high patient satisfaction and compliance, as indicated by qualitative feedback, crucial factors for long-term brace wear, treatment adherence, and success.

## P082: Presence of compensatory curve predicts postoperative curve progression in congenital scoliosis after thoracolumbar hemivertebra resection and short fusion

Yanjie Xu

1

, Li Jie Li Jie

1

, Dongyue Li

1

, Zezhang Zhu

1

, Zhen Liu

1

, Yong Qiu

1

1

Drum Tower Hospital of Nanjing University Medical School, Nanjing, China

Purpose: To investigate the impact of preoperative compensatory curve on the postoperative curve progression in congenital scoliosis (CS) patients following thoracolumbar hemivertebra (HV) resection and short fusion. Methods: This study retrospectively reviewed a consecutive cohort of patients with CS who underwent thoracolumbar HV resection and short fusion with a minimum of 2 years follow-up. According to the preoperative curve pattern, patients were divided into compensatory curve group non-compensatory curve group. Based on the postoperative coronal curve evolution, patients were further divided into the progressed group (Group P, with curve decompensation ≥ 20°) and the non-progressed group (Group NP, characterized by well-compensated curves). Results: A total of 127 patients were included in this study, with 31 patients in the compensatory curve group and 96 patients in the non-compensatory curve group. The incidence of postoperative coronal curve progression was significantly higher in the compensatory curve group than that in non-compensatory curve group (35.5% vs. 13.5%, p = 0.007). In the compensatory curve group, patients who experienced postoperative curve progression showed fewer fusion segments (p = 0.002), greater preoperative UIV translation (p = 0.003), greater preoperative LIV tilt (p = 0.017), and larger postoperative UIV tilt (p < 0.001) compared with patients in group NP. Multiple logistic regression demonstrated that the shorter fusion segments and greater postoperative UIV tilt were two independent risk factors for postoperative curve progression. Conclusion: The presence of the compensatory curve was associated with a higher incidence of postoperative curve progression in patients with CS who underwent thoracolumbar HV resection and short fusion. Shorter fusion segments and greater postoperative UIV tilt were found to be the risk factors for postoperative curve progression. Keywords: Congenital scoliosis; Compensatory curve; Hemivertebra resection; Short fusion; Coronal decompensation

## ID: 1379

## P083: Preoperative psychological evaluation in patient with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis; mental health disorders, management and recommendations

Diego Alvarez

1

, Francoise Descazeaux

1

, Carlos Huaiquilaf

1

, Karen Weissmann

2

, Carolina Gonzalez

1

1
Hospital Dr Exequiel Gonzales Cortes, Servicio de Traumatologia, Santiago, Chile, 
2
Clinica MEDS, Servicio de Traumatologia, Santiago, Chile
Introduction: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) has been associated with psychiatric disorders, which may influence disease progression and post-surgical outcomes. Evidence shows a high prevalence of psychiatric comorbidities, including somatization, intellectual disability, and stress. These psychological factors, particularly related to body self-perception, are prevalent in AIS patients, with anxiety disorders affecting 4%, behavioral disorders 3%, and mood disorders 2%. Globally, 60 million children are diagnosed with AIS, suggesting that approximately 4.2 million may experience a mental health disorder. Material and Methods: This study aimed to evaluate the presence of psychiatric pathology in AIS patients with surgical indication and to assess the percentage of patients for whom psychiatric conditions contraindicated surgery. Additionally, it sought to explore correlations between psychiatric findings and demographic variables. The study employed a retrospective, cross-sectional design, examining a cohort from a single public hospital that serves as a referral center. A total of 85 patient records were reviewed, with 77.6% of the cohort being female and the average age being 13.47 years (range 6-21). All participants were under 21 years of age, diagnosed with severe AIS, and had a surgical indication. Exclusion criteria included scoliosis of non-idiopathic origin, children under 6 years, and patients unable to undergo psychological evaluation. A comprehensive psychological assessment, developed by the hospital’s mental health team, was implemented. This assessment included three interviews per patient - two pre-surgical and one post-surgical - and utilized standardized guidelines as well as graphic projective tests for both the patient and their parents. Demographic data and interview results were collected and statistically analyzed using chi-square, Pearson, and Fisher correlation tests, with significance set at p < 0.05. Results: Of the 85 patients, 48 completed the psychological evaluation. Among them, 89.6% were approved for surgery, while 6.25% required pre-surgical psychotherapy, with anorexia nervosa being the most common cause for this intervention. Two patients (4.16%) were denied surgery due to psychiatric disorders: one with severe depressive disorder and suicidal ideation, and another with severe anxiety disorder and a lack of a support network. A statistically significant correlation was found between completing the psychological evaluation and obtaining surgical approval (p < 0.001). However, no significant correlation was observed between approval and demographic variables such as age (p = 0.0798) or gender (p = 0.531). Conclusion: In conclusion, pre-operative psychological evaluation is recommended for AIS patients with a surgical indication, as it can detect psychiatric conditions that may contraindicate surgery. In 4.26% of cases, surgery was contraindicated due to psychological factors, while 6.25% of patients required pre-surgical psychotherapy. These findings highlight the importance of comprehensive mental health screening in AIS management, although no significant correlation between psychiatric conditions and patient demographics was observed.

## P084: Application of a posterior dynamic distraction device in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis

Francoise Descazeaux

1,2,3

, Karen Weissmann

1,3

, Marcelo Perez

1

, Carlos Huaiquilaf

1,2,3

1
MEDS, Santiago, Chile,

2
Hospital Dr. Exequiel Gonzalez Cortes, Santiago, Chile,

3

Patagonia Spine Foundation, Santiago, Chile

Introduction: The Posterior Dynamic Distraction Device is a novel surgical technique designed to correct scoliotic curves while preserving spinal mobility by avoiding the need for spinal fusion. Since it does not compromise the flexibility of the spine it appears as a novel approach in the management of Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS). Material and Methods: Ten patients diagnosed with AIS and operated on between July 2022 and June 2024 using a Posterior Dynamic Distraction Device were evaluated. Preoperative clinical and radiographic outcomes were compared with postoperative and 3 months, 6 months, 1 year and 2 years follow-up results. For statistical analysis we used a t-student test with p < 0.05. Results: Of the 10 patients, 8 were female, with a mean age of 14.6 ± 1.1 years. Seventy percent of patients were involved in regular sports activities. Four patients presented with Lenke 1 curves, while six had Lenke 5 curves. Most of the cohort exhibited Risser grade 4 (n = 8) and Sanders stages 3 and 5. The mean follow-up duration was 15 ± 7 months, with 3 patients followed for 3 months, 3 for 6 months, 3 for 1 year, and 1 for 2 years. The average surgical time was 79.5 ± 15.3 minutes, with a mean blood loss of 80 ± 57 mL. Patients were discharged 48 hours postoperatively, returned to school after 18 ± 3 days, and resumed sports activities after 32.5 ± 14 days. Radiographic evaluation showed a significant reduction in the primary curve from 43.6 ± 9.3º to 21.35 ± 9.8º (p < 0.001) in the initial postoperative period. This correction was maintained at the 3-month follow-up (20 ± 9.9º, p = 0463) and remained stable at 6 months and 1 year. Similarly, the secondary curve decreased from 29 ± 5.9º to 17.8 ± 7.3º (p < 0.001), with a stable correction at 3 months (17.8 ± 7.3º, p = 0.632) and minimal change at later follow-ups. The T1-T12 height increased from 26 ± 2.6 cm to 27 ± 2.2 cm, with a sustained increase of 27 ± 1.7 cm at 3 months (p = 0.102). No significant changes were observed in kyphosis, while lordosis decreased immediately postoperatively from 51.4 ± 11.2º to 41.8 ± 12.7º,(p = 0.016) but recovered to 54.2 ± 10º at 3 months (p < 0.001), remaining stable at 6 months and 1 year. One complication occurred 1 year postoperatively due to implant failure, leading to loss of distraction. Conclusion: The Posterior Dynamic Distraction Device effectively corrects scoliosis without disrupting sagittal balance and should be considered a viable alternative for patients with Lenke 1 and 5 curves under 60º.

## ID: 1441

## P085: Management of severe scar-contracture scoliosis after necrotising fasciitis in a 13 year old child

Samir Dalvie

1

, Kshitij Chaudhary

1

1P.D. Hinduja Hospital and MRC, Spine Surgery, Mumbai, India
Introduction: Spinal deformity following scar contracture is a rare condition. It occurs when a patient experiences contracture of the lateral soft tissues in the trunk. These tissues include the skin, thoracolumbar fascia, intertransverse process ligament, abdominal wall, and paraspinal muscles. Injury to the paraspinal soft tissues, apart from the spine, can result in a mechanical imbalance that leads to scoliosis. Material and Methods: Our study presents the case of a 13-year boy who came to OPD with a deformity on his back that had been present for 6 months. He had history of necrotizing fasciitis as an infant, for which he underwent debridement and skin grafting performed by the plastic surgery team. This resulted in hypertrophic scarring on his back. The resultant deformity progressed and eventually decompensated, showing convexity to the left side in the thoracolumbar region, with higher right shoulder and hemipelvis. During the first visit, the Cobb angle was measured at 77 degrees, which progressed to 93 degrees over the next 13 months. In the first stage, an incisional release of the contracture and skin grafting were performed. Two months later, a second stage anterior spinal correction was performed from T11 to L3. Results: Immediate postoperative X-ray showed a Cobb angle of 44 degrees, indicating 47.3% correction. The final follow-up X-rays taken after 24 months showed a Cobb angle of 50 degrees, indicating a 6.4% loss of correction, but still maintaining good sagittal and coronal balance. Conclusion: An advantage of anterior approach is the avoidance of complications like infection and wound dehiscence, particularly considering the poor blood supply to scar tissue. Additionally, this approach shortens the spine and reduces the bowstring effect of the contracted tissues, which is beneficial for correcting pelvic obliquity.

## P086: Factors influencing the quality of life following posterior approach surgical treatment in adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis: a 2-year follow-up study

Nan Wu

1

, Zhengye Zhao

1

, Aoran Maheshati

1

, Shengru Wang

1

, Jianguo Zhang

1

, Deciphering Disorders Involving Scoliosis and COmorbidities Study Group

1

1

Peking Union Medical College Hospital, Beijing, China

Introduction: Posterior approach surgery is the primary method of deformity correction for patients with Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS). The goal of surgery is not only to correct deformity, but also to improve the quality of life (QoL). The Minimum Clinically Important Difference (MCID) for the SRS-22r total score is 0.4. An MCID equal to or greater than 0.4 indicates a significant improvement in the QoL during treatment. Currently, there is no research analyzing the factors influencing improved QoL based on MCID. Material and Methods: 66 patients diagnosed with AIS were prospectively included in the study, conducting a detailed phenotypic assessment. Radiological data and SRS-22r scores were assessed preoperatively and postoperatively. Based on the SRS-22r total scores, patients were divided into two groups: “I” = Improvement group (∆ Score ≥ 0.4) and “NI” = Non improvement group (∆ Score < 0.4). Univariate regression analysis was employed to identify data between the two groups, while multivariate logistic regression analysis was used to determine influencing factors. Results: In this study of 66 patients with AIS, significant improvements were observed at 2 years postoperatively compared to preoperative data. The main Cobb angle improved from 51.4 ± 13.4° to 13.4 ± 9.2° (p < 0.001), coronal balance (CB) improved from 17.6 ± 11.5 mm to 10.1 ± 7.8 mm (p < 0.001), and apical vertebral translation (AVT) improved from 43.9 ± 15.2 mm to 12.2 ± 5.5 mm (p < 0.001). The total SRS-22r scores increased from 3.9 to 4.2, with 32 patients achieving improvements equal to or greater than the MCID. Multiple logistic regression analysis identified that the influencing factor for improved QoL is the correction of the Cobb angle (p = 0.020, OR = 1.069, 95% CI = 1.011-1.132). Conclusion: Surgery via posterior approach improved both the degree of deformity and the QoL in patients with AIS. The correction of the Cobb angle is the prominent factor in QoL after surgery.

## P087: Cosmetic parameters associated with srs-22r improvement postoperatively in population with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: a 2-year follow-up study

Nan Wu

1

, Aoran Maheshati

1

, Zhengye Zhao

1

, Shengru Wang

1

, Jianguo Zhang

1

, Deciphering Disorders Involving Scoliosis and COmorbidities Study Group

1

1

Peking Union Medical College, Beijing, China

Introduction: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) significantly impacts physical appearance and quality of life. This study aims to identify cosmetic parameters associated with minimal clinical improvement in SRS-22r scores at a 2-year follow-up in AIS patients. Material and Methods: A total of 79 patients who underwent posterior spinal fusion (PSF) for AIS from February 2019 to November 2023 at PUMCH under the framework of the DISCO (Deciphering disorders Involving Scoliosis and COmorbidities, https://www.discostudy.org/) study were included. Data, including the SRS-22r questionnaire and cosmetic details were systematically gathered pre- and 2-year postoperatively. Patients were categorized by MCID values, and significant cosmetic corrections were analyzed using multivariate logistic regression to identify key contributors to SRS-22r improvement. Results: Among the 79 patients in this study, 47 had a main thoracic curve, 17 had a thoracolumbar curve, and 15 had a lumbar curve. The average age were 14.9 ± 3.0 years, mostly female (83.5%). The self-image improvement (SI) group had a lower NA of 2.82 ± 1.68°, compared to 2.24 ± 2.09° in the self-image non-improvement (SNI) group (p = 0.029). In the pain improvement (PI) group, preoperative WD was 17.64 ± 12.34 mm, significantly more than 10.90 ± 8.06 mm in the pain non-improvement (PNI) group (p = 0.009). Logistic regression analysis showed that MS correction was a primary contributor to total score improvement (OR = 1.240, p = 0.037), ATR correction to function score improvement (OR = 1.204, p = 0.022), and WD correction to pain score improvement (OR = 1.098, p = 0.017). Conclusion: In addition to shoulder balance, spinal rotation and waistline asymmetry are equally important in the clinical evaluation of AIS patients and deserve more attention.

## P088: Mental health disorders in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis surgery: prevalence trends and postoperative outcomes

Maya Abu-Zahra

1

, William Karakash

1

, Natalie Kistler

1

, David McCavitt

1

, Henry Avetisian

1

, Jeffrey C. Wang

1

, Raymond Hah

1

, R. Kiran Alluri

1

1

Keck School of Medicine of USC, Los Angeles, United States

Introduction: Current literature estimates that 7% of patients with Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS) have a mental health disorder (MHD). Anxiety is reported most frequently; other common adolescent MHDs include depressive, obsessive compulsive, eating, acute stress, attention deficit hyperactivity, and sleep disorders. The impact of AIS surgery on MHD prevalence is debated and the association of such diagnoses on post-operative complications remains largely unexplored. We aimed to determine the prevalence of MHDs in patients before and after AIS surgery, as well as to assess the effects of MHDs on postoperative complications, revision rates, and long term opioid consumption. Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted using the PearlDiver Mariner database to identify patients aged 10-18 who underwent posterior lumbar fusion with 7 or more levels for AIS between 2010-2022. Relevant diagnoses and procedures were extracted using ICD-9, ICD-10 and CPT codes. Patients under 10 or over 18 years of age, and those with malignancy, infection, or trauma were excluded. Patients were stratified based on pre-surgery MHD and matched 1:1 on age, sex, and Elixhauser Comorbidity Index (ECI). Statistical analysis employed Student's t-tests, chi-squared analyses, and McNemar's tests. Results: This study identified 9,499 patients who underwent posterior spinal fusion for AIS. MHD prevalence significantly increased from 21.3% (2,023 patients) preoperatively to 44.2% (4,199 patients) postoperatively (p < 0.001). 37.6% (2,809) of patients without previous MHD diagnosis developed a MHD after surgery. Anxiety disorders showed the most substantial increase in prevalence (12.3% to 36.0%, p < 0.001), followed by mood disorders (8.4% to 26.4%, p < 0.001). Other MHDs with significant postoperative increases included somatic disorders (0.91% to 3.0%, p < 0.001), psychotic disorders (0.75% to 2.6%, p < 0.001), and sleep disorders (0.95% to 2.06%, p < 0.001). Matched analysis produced two 1,846-patient cohorts, with a mean age of 14.8 (± 1.8) years, ECI of 1.8 (± 1.3), and 73% female. Comparison between cohorts with and without pre-surgery MHDs revealed no significant differences in long-term opioid usage, 30- and 90-day all-cause readmission, 2-year revision, or 30-day surgical complication rates. The cohort without previous MHDs demonstrated higher aggregate 30-day medical complication rates (15.5% vs 11.9%, p = 0.002). Conclusion: We found high baseline prevalence of mental health disorders in AIS patients, with a significant increase in post-surgical diagnosis. Anxiety and mood disorders were the most common conditions and exhibited the largest postoperative increases. Patients with and without pre-existing MHDs showed similar rates of postoperative surgical complications and long-term opioid usage. These findings underscore the psychological impact of surgery and the importance of comprehensive mental health screening and support for AIS patients throughout their medical treatment. Further research is needed to elucidate the factors contributing to the development of post-surgical MHDs and to develop targeted interventions to improve mental and physical outcomes in this patient population.

## P089: Effect of curve magnitude and initial brace correction on the effectiveness of conservative treatment for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis at 12 months of treatment: a randomized clinical trial

Alejandro Peiró García

1

, Victor Martin-Gorgojo

2

, Rocio García Gracía

, Imma Vilalta Vidal

Hospital Sant Joan de Déu, Esplugues de Llobregat, Spain,

2

NSW Spine Specialists, Norwest Central, Australia

Introduction: Conservative treatment of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) with full-time (FT) bracing has been shown to reduce progression and the need for surgery. Night-time (NT) bracing allows for a reduction in the number of hours worn but its effectiveness is controversial. Adherence to treatment with each type of brace is a crucial factor for success. This study aims to compare therapeutic compliance, in terms of the number of hours worn, between NT and FT braces.** Materials and Methods: A randomized clinical trial (PI20/00962) comparing FT and NT braces in AIS. The number of hours of use was analyzed by reading thermal sensors installed in the braces during successive visits at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months. Radiographic data of the main curve were analyzed at baseline, 3 months (with brace), 6 months, and 12 months using Keops software. Results: A total of 78 AIS patients were recruited, with 35 (44.87%) receiving FT treatment and 43 (55.13%) receiving NT treatment. No differences were observed regarding the effect of the initial Risser sign on curve evolution. Conclusions: Patients with a higher initial Cobb angle, higher Cobb angle on brace radiograph, or less correction with the brace compared to the initial Cobb angle are associated with a greater likelihood of progression and needing surgery.

## P090: Validity of NSQIP in pediatric spinal deformity surgery

Sabir Khan Khattak

1

1

Ghurki Trust & Teaching Hospital, Orthopedic and Spine Center, Lahore, Pakistan

Introduction: The American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (ACS-NSQIP) is a widely used tool for predicting surgical outcomes across various specialties. However, its applicability and validity in deformity spine surgery remain under-researched. Corrective surgery for adult spinal deformity (ASD) is often complex, involving a high risk of complications due to factors like patient age, comorbidities, and the extensive nature of the procedures. Assessing the validity of NSQIP in predicting postoperative outcomes in deformity spine surgery is crucial to determining its reliability and accuracy in this specialized field. Our objective is to evaluate the likelihood of postoperative complications and mortality in pediatric patients undergoing corrective surgery for spinal deformity using the Surgical Risk Calculator (SRC) from the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (ACS-NSQIP). Material and Methods: A prospective analysis was done on 175 pediatric patients who underwent corrective surgery for spinal deformity, meeting the inclusion criteria at the Department of Orthopedics & Spine Centre, Ghurki Trust Teaching Hospital, Lahore. We preoperatively assess the patients using the National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (ACS-NSQIP) to predict risk factors associated with admission, as well as a prolonged length of stay following surgery. Results: There were majority of female cases compared to males, with ages ranging from 7-16 years. The majority (46.8%) had a BMI < 20 kg/m2. Preoperative risk factors were observed among these patients as asthma, Structural pulmonary abnormality, development stay, neuromuscular disorders and nutritional requirement. 29.8% of ICU patients stayed for more than 2 days. The overall rate of 30-day complications was 9.5%, with a mortality rate of 0.3%, a morbidity rate of 8.5%, a reoperation rate of 3.5%, and a readmission rate of 3.85%. Morbidity was highest in the neuromuscular group and lowest in the idiopathic group. Compared to posterior fusions, anterior fusions and those extending to the pelvis were linked to higher complication rates. Risk factors for complications included hepatobiliary disease, cognitive impairment, elevated American Society of Anesthesiologists class, and prolonged operative time. Conclusion: The ACS-NSQIP Surgical Risk Calculator is a valuable tool for predicting postoperative complications in pediatric spinal deformity surgery. Higher morbidity was seen in patients with neuromuscular disorders and in those undergoing anterior fusions or surgeries extending to the pelvis. Preoperative risk factors like hepatobiliary disease, cognitive impairment, elevated ASA class, and prolonged operative time were significant predictors of complications.

## P091: Nutritional status of patients undergoing spinal fusion surgery at a pediatric reference hospital in Northeastern Brazil

Rebeca Chaves

1

, Alexia Sousa

1

, Dielson Sousa

, Bruna Ferreira

3

Federal University of Ceará, Fortaleza, Brazil

Introduction: A major surgical procedure triggers a catabolic response, which can worsen in the presence of malnutrition. Malnutrition is recognized as a risk factor for adverse postoperative outcomes1. Among major surgical procedures, spinal fusion surgery stands out as a surgical correction for spinal deformity. In this surgery, monitoring nutritional status is essential to detect nutritional deficits early as a measure to ensure a good surgical outcome2. Material and Methods: This was a cross-sectional, descriptive study conducted at Hospital Infantil Albert Sabin, a pediatric reference hospital in the state of Ceará, Brazil. The study period was from February 2023 to August 2024, including children and adolescents aged 9 to 17 years, candidates for elective spinal fusion surgery, of both sexes. The variables analyzed were: age (A), sex, origin, surgical time, weight, height (H), body mass index (BMI), and anthropometric parameters of BMI/A and H/A according to the World Health Organization (WHO). The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Ethics Committee of Hospital Infantil Albert Sabin (CAEE: 81691924.6.0000.5042). Descriptive analysis was presented, and the difference between means was analyzed using Student's t-test. Analyses were performed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS), version 22, considering statistical significance at p < 0.05. Results: The study sample consisted of 28 patients, 4 males (14.3%) and 24 females (85.7%). The mean age was 14.5 years (sd = 1.71), with 21 patients (76.6%) from rural areas and 6 (23.3%) from the capital and metropolitan region. The mean surgical time was 8 hours, 15 minutes, and 55 seconds. A significantly longer surgical time was observed for boys (10 hours, 11 minutes) compared to girls (7 hours, 33 minutes) (p = 0.01). Of the surgical interventions, 9 (15%) developed complications, such as surgical site infections (SSI), wound dehiscence, respiratory complications, and SSI reoperation. Regarding anthropometric data, the mean BMI was 21.5 kg/m2. Nutritional diagnosis was based on the BMI/A parameter, with 3 patients (10.7%) classified as underweight, 15 (53.7%) as normal weight, and 10 (35.7%) as obese. According to the H/A parameter, 7 patients (25%) were classified as short stature, and 21 (75%) had appropriate height for their age. Among the sexes, underweight was more prevalent in boys (50%) compared to girls (4.1%), while 62.5% of girls were of normal weight (p = 0.09). Conclusion: Most patients were of normal weight; however, a significant percentage had an inadequate nutritional status. Therefore, early nutritional monitoring is essential, considering that this surgery, by its nature, causes metabolic alterations and increases energy demands, which may raise the risks and lead to unfavorable surgical outcomes.

Studies in health technology and informatics, 280, 235–240. https://doi.org/10.3233/SHTI210475

## P092: Clinical and epidemiological profile of patients undergoing spinal fusion surgery in a pediatric referral hospital in Northeastern Brazil

Jose Alberto Oliveira

1

, Alexia Sousa

2

, Rebeca Chaves

3

, Dielson Sousa

4

, Bruna Ferreira

5

, Cibele Maia

6

1
Hospital Infantil Albert Sabin, Orthopedic Surgeon, Fortaleza, Brazil,

2
Hospital Infantil Albert Sabin, Psychology, Fortaleza, Brazil,

3
Hospital Infantil Albert Sabin, Nutrition, Fortaleza, Brazil,

4
Hospital Infantil Albert Sabin, Stomatherapy Nursing, Fortaleza, Brazil,

5
Hospital Infantil Albert Sabin, Physiotherapy, Fortaleza,

6

Hospital Infantil Albert Sabin, Pediatrician, Fortaleza, Brazil

Introduction: The word scoliosis comes from the Greek skolios, meaning curved. It is a three-dimensional deformity of the spine (coronal, sagittal, and axial planes), defined by a lateral curvature greater than 10° calculated by the Cobb method on an anteroposterior (AP) radiograph1-2. Regarding etiology, scoliosis can be classified as idiopathic, congenital, neuromuscular, or syndromic. It is a significant risk factor for the development of postoperative pulmonary complications, as well as for the difficulty in restoring pulmonary function after deformity correction3. It is worth mentioning that perioperative management of patients with scoliosis requires a multidisciplinary approach to improve outcomes, reduce the risk of complications, prevent neurological injuries, minimize blood loss, and optimize postoperative care. Materials and Methods: This is an epidemiological, cross-sectional, descriptive study that assessed the sociodemographic profile and multidisciplinary follow-up of children and adolescents who underwent spinal fusion surgery in a referral hospital within the public health network of the State of Ceará, Brazil, from February 2023 to August 2024. The study was conducted at Albert Sabin Children's Hospital, a tertiary care center specializing in pediatric care and a referral center for the State of Ceará and neighboring states in northeastern Brazil. Care for patients with spinal deformities began in 2023, offering both surgical and multidisciplinary outpatient care (orthopedics, nursing, physiotherapy, psychology, and nutrition) aimed at providing comprehensive patient care. The first contact with the service is made by the orthopedic surgeon, who makes referrals for patient navigation. Data were collected from multidisciplinary care records. The following variables were recorded: age, sex, residence, diagnosis, date of the procedure, procedure performed, and whether there were complications. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 20 and presented as absolute and percentage frequencies. The research project was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Albert Sabin Children's Hospital (CAEE: 81691924.6.0000.5042). Results: From February 2023 to August 2024, 60 (100%) surgical procedures were performed. Of these, 4 (6.7%) patients were seen by psychology, 28 (46.7%) by nutrition, and 0 by nursing and physiotherapy. Regarding sociodemographic data, 54 (90%) were female, the mean age was 14.5, with a median of 15 years. A total of 76.6% were from rural areas, and 23.3% from the capital and metropolitan region. The mean surgical time was 8 hours, 15 minutes, and 55 seconds. Of the surgical interventions performed, 9 (15%) developed complications such as surgical site infections, wound dehiscence, MARSI (Medical Adhesive-Related Skin Injuries), respiratory complications, and reoperation for wound site. Conclusion: The interdisciplinary approach in this field is still incipient. However, it has been observed that integrating interdisciplinarity in complex clinical conditions is essential for the success of therapeutic management, especially in the perioperative care of patients with spinal deformities.

Introduction: To estimate the time from initial visit to surgery in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) patients and the main reasons for the delay in a multicenter study. Material and Methods: This retrospective study evaluated 509 patients with AIS from 16 hospitals across six Latin American countries. From each hospital´s deformity registry, the following patient data were extracted: demographics, main curve Cobb angle, Lenke Classification at the initial visit and time of surgery, time from indication-for-surgery to surgery, curve progression, Risser skeletal-maturity score and causes for surgical cancelation or delay. Surgeons were asked if they needed to change the original surgical plan due to curve progression. Data also were collected on each hospital’s waiting list numbers and mean delay to AIS surgery. Results: 66.8% of the patients waited over six months and 33.9% over a year. Waiting time was not impacted by the patient’s age when surgery first became indicated (p = 0.22) but waiting time did differ between countries (p < 0.001) and hospitals (p < 0.001). Time delay to surgery was significantly associated with increasing magnitude of the Cobb angle through the second year of waiting (p < 0.001). Reported causes for delay were hospital-related (48.4%), economic (47.3%), and logistic (4.2%). Oddly, waiting time for surgery did not correlate with the hospital's reported waiting-list lengths (p = 0.57). Conclusion: Prolonged waits for AIS surgery are common in Latin America, with rare exceptions. At most centers, patients wait over six months, most commonly for economic and hospital-related reasons. Whether this directly impacts surgical outcomes in Latin America still must be studied.

## ID: 2331

## P094: Low density versus high density screw in Lenke I scoliosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis

Bin Zheng

1

1

Peking University People's Hospital, Spine Surgery, Beijing, China

Introduction: This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of low-density versus high-density pedicle screw in Lenke I AIS patients through systematic review and meta-analysis. Methods: A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase databases. Studies comparing low-density and high-density pedicle screw in Lenke I AIS patients were included. Two authors independently selected studies, assessed risk of bias, and extracted data. Meta analysis were performed using RevMan 5.4 software. Results: Eleven studies involving 697 patients (397 in the low-density group and 300 in the high-density group) were included. Meta-analysis showed no significant differences between low-density and high-density groups in terms of blood loss, operative time, complication rates, or revision rates. Radiographic outcomes, including major Cobb angle, curve correction, thoracic kyphosis, coronal and sagittal balance, were also similar between the two groups. However, the low-density group was associated with significantly lower costs. Conclusion: This meta-analysis suggests that low-density pedicle screw can achieve similar clinical and radiographic outcomes compared to high-density constructs in Lenke I AIS patients, while potentially reducing costs.

Introduction: Restoration of the ideal sagittal alignment is essential in AIS deformity correction. ## P101: Novel reconstruction plate augmentation technique for treatment of myelomeningocele associated severe kyphotic deformity: a case series

Sree Vemu

1

, Austin Nguyen

1

, Zachary Diltz

1

, David Bauer

2

, Darrell Hanson

1

1
Houston Methodist Hospital, Orthopedic Surgery, Houston, United States,

2

Texas Children's Hospital, Neurosurgery, Houston, United States

Introduction: Patients with myelomeningocele (MMC) and severe kyphotic gibbus deformities experience difficulties with sitting and lying flat, leading to increased skin breakdown and risk of infection. Many patients undergo kyphectomy, cordotomy, and long-segment posterior spinal instrumentation using well-established techniques, such as Fackler, to correct sagittal alignment. However, these treatments still face very high rates of hardware failure and wound issues. Dynamic Compression (DCP) AO reconstruction plates have been successfully used in other areas of orthopedics to provide additional stability, fracture reduction, and promote bony healing. Objectives: This case series presents a novel technique using DCP AO reconstruction plates to augment posterior spinal constructs in patients with MMC-associated kyphotic deformities. Methods: Three patients were treated with kyphectomy, cordotomy, posterior fusion, and augmentation using contoured DCP AO plates. Two patients underwent the Fackler technique, which involved placing titanium rods into the S1 foramen with cantilever bending to correct the kyphotic deformity. Results: All patients demonstrated successful outcomes. The first patient, with a 31-degree kyphotic deformity and T12-L1 non-union, underwent T4-pelvis fusion and achieved stable correction at two-year follow-up without hardware failure or wound complications. The second patient, with a 160-degree mid-thoracic gibbus deformity, underwent L1-4 kyphectomy and T10-pelvis fusion using the Fackler technique and a DCP AO reconstruction plate. Postoperative results showed stable deformity correction and no complications. The third patient, with a 170-degree thoracolumbar gibbus deformity, underwent L2-L5 kyphectomy and T9-sacrum fusion with the Fackler technique and augmentation using a DCP AO reconstruction plate. At both one- and two-year follow-ups, the patient had no wound breakdown, hardware failure, or the need for revision surgery. Surgical Technique: After positioning and spinal cord monitoring, posterior incisions were made, and scar tissue from previous surgeries was meticulously removed. Pedicle screws were placed bilaterally using stereotactic navigation. Vertebral body resections were performed, and the Fackler technique was employed to insert titanium rods for deformity correction. DCP AO plates were contoured and applied to augment fixation, followed by bone grafting to promote fusion. Conclusion: The use of a DCP AO reconstruction plate offers a promising augmentation strategy for managing severe kyphotic deformities in MMC patients. Further studies are needed to assess long-term outcomes and broader applicability of this approach.

Emilson Camapum

Introduction: Kyphosis associated with myelomeningocele is a debilitating condition linked to progressive deformity, recurrent skin lesions, and a decline in quality of life. Surgical treatment is complex. The aim of this study is to evaluate the long-term outcomes and complications of patients undergoing surgery with follow-up greater than 5 years. Material and Methods: Patients who consecutively underwent kyphosis surgery at the same institution between 2014 and 2020 were evaluated retrospectively regarding their outcomes and complications. Surgical indication was based on progressive deformity and/or recurrent skin ulcers at the apex of the kyphosis. Patients with less than 5 years of follow-up were excluded. Results: During this period, 9 patients underwent kyphosis surgery associated with myelomeningocele, with a mean follow-up of 84.1 ± 23 months (ranging from 60 to 115 months). All patients presented with hydrocephalus and were using ventriculoperitoneal shunts. The fourth patient experienced rod breakage and pseudarthrosis, requiring revision and supplemental anterior arthrodesis. No patient presented with skin lesions at the apex of the kyphosis throughout the follow-up, and there was overall functional improvement in patient positioning and mobility. Conclusion: This series with a long follow-up period demonstrated the efficacy of kyphosis surgery, which was maintained in the long term even in patients with complications and removal of instrumentation.

## P103: Progressive curve straightening and overcorrection occur in skeletally immature patients after anterior instrumented fusion for thoracic scoliosis - Is this 'the ultimate tether'?

Gin Way Law

1

, Glenys Poon

, Sunwoo Sunny Kim

2

, John Ruiz

, Leok Lim Lau

1

, Gabriel Liu

1

, Hee Kit Wong

2

National University of Singapore, Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, Singapore, Singapore

Introduction: Anterior fusions are not common commonly performed for the correction of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS). Although fusion surgeries are thought to correct spinal deformity with immediate cessation of growth in the instrumented segments, progressive continued curve correction has been shown in some of our patients that have undergone thoracoscopic anterior fusion for correction of AIS. This study aims to investigate the incidence of this phenomenon, and to establish the impact of skeletal immaturity along with other factors related. Material and Methods: We performed a retrospective review of thoracoscopic single-rod fusions of AIS Lenke 1 curves in female patients aged 11-20 years old performed between June 2000-July 2013 with a minimum follow up of 5 years. Patients with post-operative screw pullouts were excluded. Skeletally immature patients with Risser scores 0-3 at time of surgery (Group 1) were compared to those with skeletally more mature patients with Risser scores 4-5 (Group 2). The outcome measures assessed included curve changes over time, rod angle changes, complications, and re-operation rates. Results: 39 patients were identified over the mean follow-up timeframe of 96.0 months. 19 of the 39 patients had rod straightening (> 5°), of which 15 were in Group 1 and 4 were in Group 2 (p < 0.001). 19 patients had Risser scores 0-3 (Group 1), and 20 patients had Risser scores 4-5 (Group 2) at the time of surgery. Both groups showed (i) similar preoperative coronal (main thoracic curve sizes and flexibility, proximal thoracic and lumbar curves, clavicle angles, C7-central sacral vertical lines) and sagittal (sagittal vertical axis, thoracic kyphosis, lumbar lordosis) parameters, (ii) similar perioperative data (length of surgery, duration of hospital stay, blood loss), and (iii) similar post-operative curve correction and magnitude of the adjacent non-structural proximal thoracic and lumbar curves (p > 0.05). The post-operative instrumented Cobbs angle of the main thoracic curve in Group 1 were 10.7 ± 4.5° and 10.2 ± 5.4° in Group 2 on immediate post operative radiographs (p = 0.745). Group 1 showed a 6.9 ± 2.7° mean angular change of the rods with rod straightening compared to Group 2 with 4.0 ± 2.1° (p < 0.001), with corresponding improvements in Cobbs angle correction over time at 5.3 ± 2.2° versus 3.0 ± 2.6° respectively (p = 0.006). Curve straightening of the instrumented levels in Group 1 started within 6 months from surgery with continued improvements seen up to 5 years post surgery (p < 0.05). There was no significant change in the instrumented curves in Group 2 beyond 1 year post surgery (p > 0.05). All other coronal and sagittal parameters were otherwise similar between the groups at last follow up. (p > 0.05) Both groups showed similar complication profiles including adding on, loss of correction (> 5°), rod breakage, and (iv) reoperation rates (p > 0.05). Conclusion: Post-operative rod and curve straightening occurs progressively, and more commonly in skeletally immature patients without increase in adverse outcomes in thoracoscopic single-rod fusions for AIS correction.

## P104: How does exercise therapy change paraspinal muscle activation patterns in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis patients? - A systematic review

Hao Wu

1

, Prudence Cheung

1

, Kwai Lam Loh

1

, Teng Zhang

1

, Jason Cheung

1

1

The University of Hong Kong, Department of Orthopaedics & Traumatology, Hong Kong SAR, Hong Kong

Introduction: Various types of exercise therapy have been reported for the management of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS), including weight training, core stabilization exercises, and scoliosis-specific exercises (SSEs). However, the specific movement components in exercise therapy that induce muscle activation patterns that support the correction of the scoliotic curve, also known as positive correction pattern, remains unclear. In this systematic review, we therefore asked: 1) What are the immediate effects of exercise therapy for scoliosis on paraspinal muscle activation patterns measured by surface electromyography (sEMG) in patients with AIS? 2) What are the effects of long-term exercise therapy intervention on paraspinal muscle activation patterns measured by sEMG in patients with AIS? Eligible articles were published from 1990 to 2024. In these databases, we searched for titles, abstracts, and keywords using key search items including (idiopathic scoliosis) AND (exercise OR physio* OR rehabilitation) AND (Electromyo*) NOT (surgery). The main parameters extracted from the studies included study design, age of the subjects, average Cobb angles, control group, muscle group of focus, exercise therapy interventions, testing movements for sEMG, and time of the sEMG test. In addition, the duration of long-term exercise therapy intervention was also extracted. The main outcomes extracted from the studies were scores used to describe convex/concave sEMG ratios and changes in convex/concave sEMG ratios induced by exercise therapy. The quality of included studies was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Results: 20 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included. 6 studies focused on the immediate effects of asymmetric exercise therapy movements on paraspinal muscle activation pattern. 5 studies focused on the immediate effect of symmetric exercise therapy movements. Symmetric movement components of exercise therapy, such as prone or supine spinal extension, seem to reduce the convex/concave sEMG ratio measured in habitual sitting or standing. 7 studies investigated changes in paraspinal muscle activation pattern induced by long-term exercise therapy program. Long-term exercise therapy intervention in general leads to a lower convex/concave sEMG ratio. Conclusion: Studies with moderate quality of evidence showed that symmetric movements are worth including in an exercise therapy program for scoliosis, as these movements facilitate a balanced muscle activation pattern and improved core stability. Given the diverse range of exercise therapy types resulting from the lack of consensus, and the potential for asymmetric movements to selectively engage muscles on the concave or convex side, further research is needed for asymmetric components of exercise therapy with specific curve types clearly specified. sEMG biofeedback training can be a future direction to quantitatively study exercise therapy movements for scoliosis using new technologies like computer vision and lightweight sEMG sensors to monitor movements during therapy, particularly in unsupervised home settings.

## P105: Surgical correction of scoliosis in osteogenesis imperfecta

Andre Castilho

1

, Pedro Torres

1

, Rodrigo Cruzeiro

1

, Matheus Vieira

1

, Mauricio Cardoso

1

1

Hospital Unimed, Belo Horizonte, Brazil

Introduction: Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is a bone dysplasia caused by a genetic disorder of type 1 collagen synthesis, found mainly in bones, ligaments, teeth, and sclera. It is a heterogeneous disease with various genotypes and phenotypes and presents with varying degrees of tissue involvement and severity. It primarily affects long bones, but in more severe cases can affect the spine, with scoliosis being one of the main manifestations. The objective of this work is to report the clinical case of a patient with type XII OI with scoliosis who underwent surgical treatment with isolated posterior arthrodesis. Materials and Methods: We report the case of a male patient, 11 years and 5 months old, diagnosed with Sillence type XII OI, in outpatient follow-up for double curve scoliosis. On radiographic examinations, a thoracic curve of 94° (T2 to T11) and a lumbar curve of 70° (T11 to L5) were observed on the sitting AP radiograph, and kyphosis of 52° (T5 to L2) on the sitting lateral radiograph. On manual traction, the curves in the coronal plane showed partial flexibility, correcting to 58 and 48°, respectively. No pelvic obliquity was observed on radiography. Clinical examination revealed a weight of 28 kilograms, height of 113 cm, wheelchair-bound, and a history of multiple fractures - 30 reported - with 3 previous surgeries, including two long bone osteosyntheses and one surgical revision. Results: Initially, Pamidronate was administered preoperatively. Arthrodesis from T2 to L5 instrumented with pedicle screws and titanium rods was performed via an isolated posterior approach. Ponte osteotomies at the apex of the thoracic curve were performed for release and gain of flexibility at the time of correction, which was considered satisfactory. Use of pediatric material was necessary, such as screws with smaller head profiles and smaller diameters, and no cement was used in the screws. The procedure occurred without complications, and postoperatively there was good pain control and seated balance. At the 2-year follow-up, radiological consolidation of the arthrodesis was observed, without loss of curve correction or instrumentation failure. Conclusion: Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is considered the most common hereditary connective tissue disease, causing a range of osteoarticular alterations, including scoliosis, which can affect 39 to 90% of these patients. The need for surgical correction of scoliosis in this population is common and aims to control pain, restore stability, and, above all, halt curve progression. However, surgical correction and, especially, its maintenance over time are challenging due to the poor bone quality of these patients. In the present case, correction was maintained at the 2-year follow-up. This good evolution is most likely due to the use of posterior instrumentation with pedicle screws, which allow greater fixation and rigidity to the system, and the use of Pamidronate preoperatively, which improves bone quality, increasing the pull-out strength of the screws. Despite high complication rates reported in the literature, none were observed either intraoperatively or postoperatively in this analyzed case.

## P106: Is preoperative magnetic resonance really necessary in non-severe idiopathic scoliosis? a retrospective study

Giovanni Ciani

1

, Francesco Vommaro

1

, Chiara Cini

1

, Konstantinos Martikos

1

, Luca Boriani

1

, Alessandro Gasbarrini

1

1

Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Bologna

Introduction: This retrospective study investigates the use of preoperative whole-spine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in patients with non-severe idiopathic scoliosis. The aim was to investigate the role of preoperative MRI in the prevention of correction-related complication in idiopathic scoliosis. Methods: We enrolled 300 patients (250 females, 50 males) with an average age of 14 years (range 10-18 years) who underwent scoliosis correction with posterior standard fusion surgery from June 2018 to June 2024. Inclusion criteria were age less than 18 years old, Coronal Cobb angles degrees equal or less than 70° and a minimum of 24-month follow-up period. Patients with congenital scoliosis or neuromuscular scoliosis were excluded. All participants were asymptomatic for central or peripheral neurological symptoms. Results: MRI findings revealed spinal cord anomalies in 42 patients (14%): 31 with thoracic or thoraco-lumbar syringomyelia, 10 with Arnold-Chiari malformation type 1, and 1 with tethered cord syndrome. In two cases syringomyelia was found to be related to Arnold-Chiari malformation but no decompression of hindbrain disorder was required. Six cases of syringomyelia were significant in size and volume; however, neurosurgical evaluations determined that no surgical intervention was necessary. The patient with tethered cord underwent a successful neurosurgical release prior to scoliosis surgery. All patients subsequently underwent standard posterior spinal fusion without intraoperative or postoperative complications over a follow-up period ranging from 3 months to 6 years. Results indicated a higher incidence of myeloradicular abnormalities among male patients, those with left thoracic curves, and patients with short segment curves. The overall incidence of spinal cord anomalies in non-severe idiopathic scoliosis was low (10%), and none posed a contraindication to scoliosis surgery. Conclusion: In conclusion, preoperative MRI is essential in severe scoliosis cases but its routine use in non-severe idiopathic scoliosis may be limited to patients presenting with specific risk factors, such as male gender, primary thoracic curve, or left thoracic curve. Given the retrospective nature and limited sample size of this study, further research is needed to establish more robust guidelines for MRI use in non-severe idiopathic scoliosis.

## P107: Comparison of physical activities versus conventional therapy on patients with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: systematic review and met-analysis

Ahmed Jahwari

1,2

, Hanaa Al Alawi

3

, Mohamed Othman

4

, Yaqoub Al Mufargi

4

1
Medical City for Military and Security Services, Spine Services, Muscat, Oman, 
2
Medical City for Military and Security Services, Spine and Orthopoedics, Muscat, Oman, 
3
Medical City for Military and Security Services, Muscat, Oman, 
4
Medical City for Military and Security Services, Muscat, Oman
Introduction: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a spinal deformity with an unknown etiology. Bracing was considered as the main treatment option for patients with mild to moderate curve, however there is sparse evidence showing positive role of physical exercises in reducing and maintaining curve progression. The aim of this study is to show via systematic review and meta-analysis the effectiveness of physical exercises in reducing Cobb angle compared to conventional therapy. Material and Methods: Studies were collected from PubMed, MEDLINE, Cochrane library and Google Scholar. Key search words included are AIS, adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, PSSE, exercise, Schroth, bracing, core strengthening, Cobb angle. Results: The pooled effect size (standardized mean difference, SMD) was favoring the Schroth method for reducing the Cobb angle in the meta-analysis. The pooled SMD was -0.78 (95% CI: -1.55, -0.02). ## P108: Pott’s kyphosis in a 15 month old child treated with decompression and non- instrumented fusion. Case report and clinical outcome

Alejandro Nicolás Coombes

1

, Guillermo Kahl

1

, Nicolas Albarracin

1

, Osvaldo Romano

1

, Mario Olivera

1

, Maria Dolores Posadas

1

, Elmer Layme Galarza

1

, Federico Ramanzin

1

1

Hospital de Alta Complejidad El Cruce, Buenos Aires, Argentina

Introduction: Spinal tuberculosis (TB) also known as Pott’s disease, is the most common manifestation of osteoarticular tuberculosis. There are many predisposing factors and population groups with increased risk of spinal TB, such as immunocompromised people, children, the elderly, and immigrants from endemic countries. Affecting about a quarter of the world’s population, TB is a global health problem and a significant cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. It is usually insidious in onset and is often difficult to discern in the differential diagnosis, often causing long delays in diagnosis. The disease usually manifests as back pain with some systemic symptoms, such as intermittent fever, night sweats or weight loss. Due to the nonspecific clinical presentation of the disease, a high index of suspicion is essential. Pott's disease is the most dangerous form of skeletal tuberculosis, as it can cause bone destruction, deformity, and paraplegia. Material and Methods: A clinical and imaging review is performed on a 15-month-old patient referred from another institution due to a history of recent sepsis associated with a lung abscess that required drainage in the context of SARS COVID + with respiratory failure that required mechanical ventilatory assistance for 74 days post intubation placement of tracheostomy, presenting during hospitalization the development of a painful dorsal hump. Supported with bilevel continuous positive airway pressure (BiPAP), nutritional deficiency with low weight (8.6 kg), incomplete immunization, and history of multifamily housing. Multiple biopsy samples were taken by bone puncture and sent for culture, where results were obtained for Staphylococcus aureus and CSF puncture with positive culture and GeneXpert + for mycobacteria. Antibiotic regimen Ethambutol, Isoniazid Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide was started. Neurological examination difficult to perform due to the patient's age, mobility of four limbs preserved. On X-ray images, an acute angle kyphosis was observed at the level of D6 (65°). On CT images, destruction of the vertebral body with compression of the spinal canal with epidural collection with soft tissue abscess with medullary edema was evident in MRI sequences. Results: The treatment chosen for active TB infection was to perform a dorsal decompressive laminectomy, wide debridement, and placement of autologous bone obtained from the iliac crest. The child was underweight and due to the difficulty in obtaining a fixation system, a non-instrumented fusion was chosen, which was performed under continuous electrophysiological monitoring. Subsequently, antibiotic treatment and external support with a cast were continued, and the patient was later transferred to an orthosis. The clinical evolution was good, with complete improvement of symptoms without associated neurological damage and recovery of gait pattern. Conclusion: In the presence of vertebral destruction, abscess, severe deformity or neurological compromise, surgical treatment is mandatory. Any surgical approach that provides stability to prevent progression of kyphotic deformity is indicated even in very young children.

## P109: The effect of employing the Jackson technique as a pelvic anchor in adult spinal deformity surgery on the progression of hip osteoarthritis

Kazumichi Yagura

1

, Shu Takahashi

1

, Kazuyuki Segami

1

, Yusuke Oshita

2

, Koji Kanzaki

1

, Tomoaki Toyone

3

, Yoshifumi Kudo

3

1
Showa University Fujigaoka Hospital, Orthopaedic Surgery, Yokohama-city, Kanagawa, Japan,

2
Showa University Northern Yokohama Hospital, Orthopaedic Surgery, Yokohama-city, Kanagawa, Japan,

3

Showa University School of Medicine, Orthopaedic Surgery, Shinagawa-ku, Tokyo, Japan

Introduction: The S1 pedicle screw (PS), iliac screw (IS), or S2-alar-iliac (S2AI) screw is commonly used as a pelvic anchor in adult spinal deformity (ASD) surgery. However, adjacent segment disease is an unavoidable complication of long spinal fusion. Recent studies have suggested that sacroiliac joint fixation may contribute to the progression of hip osteoarthritis (OA). At our institution, the Jackson technique (intrasacral fixation) was previously used as a pelvic anchor in ASD surgery. We hypothesized that this technique could mitigate the postoperative progression of hip OA owing to the preservation of sacroiliac joint movement compared to cases using IS or S2AI screws. We aimed to radiographically evaluate the progression of hip OA in patients who underwent ASD surgery combined with The Jackson technique. Material and Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 16 patients (32 hip joints) who underwent ASD surgery using the Jackson technique from 2017 to 2022. The joint space width (JSW) in the central space of the hip, center edge (CE) angle, and sharp angle were measured. The radiographic progression of hip OA was defined as a reduction of more than 0.5 mm/year in JSW. Results: The mean patient age was 67.3 years, with a mean follow-up period of 50.6 months. The mean number of fixation segments was 9.1. The respective preoperative and final follow-up visit measurements, which were not significantly different, were as follows: JSW, 4.5 mm and 4.2 mm; CE angle, 29.4° and 31.0°; and sharp angle, 41.5° and 39.8°. Conclusion: In a previous study, the rate of joint space narrowing in cases where an IS or S2AI screw fixation was used for long spinal fusion was 0.31 mm/year. Another study suggested that 58% of patients with ASD who underwent sacroiliac joint fixation experienced hip OA progression one year after surgery. Our results demonstrated a lower progression rate of hip OA compared to previous reports, indicating that sacroiliac joint movement preservation could prevent hip OA progression. However, some patients required the replacement of Jackson rods with IS or S2AI screws because of distal junctional failure. The Jackson technique should be selected after considering the bone quality and extent of fixation.

## P110: To correct or not to correct: fracture on degenerative scoliosis

Adnene Benammou

1,2

, Souha Bennour

1,2

, Seddik Akremi

1,2

, Amal Abayed

1,2

, Mehdi Bellil

1,2

, Mohamed Ben Salah

1,2

1
University Tunis el Manar, Faculty of Medecine of Tunis, Tunis, Tunisia,

2

Charles Nicolle Hospital, Orthopedic Surgery Department, Tunis, Tunisia

Introduction: Thoracolumbar fractures of the spine are common, and their management is well-documented according to different classification systems. However, the occurrence of these fractures in the onset of degenerative scoliosis has not been reported in literature. Material and Methods: This is a case report of a 73-year-old active male who sustained a work injury following a fall from a tree with an estimated height of 2 meters. Results: The patient presented initially at a local hospital with multilevel trauma with a hemopneumothorax needing a chest tube and a spinal injury. After a 12-day intensive-care-unit stay, the patient was transferred to our department. Initial examination found a bilateral motor deficit classified as ASIA C. Imaging found a type C fracture of the L1L2 Vertebras according to the AO Classification on a pre-existing degenerative spinal deformity with multilevel degenerative disk disease and foraminal stenosis. Because he was a high-risk patient and reported no previous complaint related to degenerative disk disease, we opted to treat the traumatic lesion alone. The patient benefited from a laminectomy with long segment fixation. At last, follow up the patient presented with a clean wound and partial neurological recovery. He was able to ambulate with aid. Conclusion: Degenerative scoliosis poses a therapeutic challenge especially in older patients where management opposes conservative treatment with focal surgery alone to taking the “opportunity” of the fracture to correct the deformity with multilevel fusion. There were no reported cases of type C fractures occurring on degenerative deformity spine although there were reports of fractures on intreated idiopathic scoliosis where the authors suggested that the goal was to establish the anatomy previous to the fracture. In our case, we opted to treat the fracture alone thus to reestablish the previous anatomy. Management of such fractures must take in consideration the patient complaints and the comorbidities that may make an extensive surgery not tolerated.

## P111: Precise execution of personalized surgical planning using three-dimensional printed guide template in severe and complex adult spinal deformity patients requiring three-column osteotomy: a retrospective, comparative matched-cohort study

Yangpu Zhang

1

, Honghao Yang

1

, Yong Hai

1

1

Beijing Chao-Yang Hospital, Capital Medical University, Beijing, China

Introduction: The surgical treatment of severe and complex adult spinal deformity (ASD) commonly required three-column osteotomy (3-CO), which was technically demanding with high risk of neurological deficit. Personalized three dimensional (3D)-printed guide template based on preoperative planning has been gradually applied in 3-CO procedure. The purpose of this study was to compare the efficacy, safety, and precision of 3D-printed osteotomy guide template and free-hand technique in the treatment of severe and complex ASD patients requiring 3-CO. Material and Methods: This was a single-centre retrospective comparative cohort study of patients with severe and complex ASD (Cobb angle of scoliosis > 80° with flexibility < 25% or focal kyphosis > 90°) who underwent posterior spinal fusion and 3-CO between January 2020 to January 2023, with a minimum 12 months follow-up. Personalized computer-assisted three-dimensional osteotomy simulation was performed for all recruited patients, who were further divided into template and non-template groups based on the application of 3D-printed osteotomy guide template according to the surgical planning. Patients in the two groups were age- and gender- propensity-matched. The radiographic parameters, postoperative neurological deficit, and precision of osteotomy execution were compared between groups. Results: A total of 40 patients (age 36.53 ± 11.98 years) were retrospectively recruited, with 20 patients in each group. The preoperative focal kyphosis (FK) was 92.72° ± 36.77° in the template group and 93.47° ± 33.91° in the non-template group, with a main curve Cobb angle of 63.35° (15.00°, 92.25°) and 64.00° (20.25°, 99.20°), respectively. However, the match ratio of execution to simulation osteotomy angle was significantly greater in the template group than the non-template group (coronal: 89.90% vs. 74.50%, p < 0.001; sagittal: 90.45% vs. 80.35%, p < 0.001). The operating time (ORT) was significantly shorter (359.25 ± 57.79 min vs. 398.90 ± 59.48 min, p = 0.039) and the incidence of postoperative neurological deficit (5.0% vs. 35.0%, p = 0.018) was significantly lower in the template group than the non-template group. Conclusion: Performing 3-CO with the assistance of personalized 3D-printed guide template could increase the precision of execution, decrease the risk of postoperative neurological deficit, and shorten the ORT in the correction surgery for severe and complex ASD. The personalized osteotomy guide had the advantages of 3D insight of the case-specific anatomy, identification of osteotomy location, and translation of the surgical planning or simulation to the real surgical site.

## P112: Biomechanical analysis of spinal cord injury during scoliosis correction surgery

Junyu Li

1

, Zekun Li

, Yilin Lu

, Xiang Zhang

, Yongqiang Wang

1

, Weishi Li

1

, Miao Yu

1

1

Peking University Third Hospital of China, Beijing, China

Introduction: Surgical correction is a common treatment for severe scoliosis. Due to the significant spinal deformation that occurs with this condition, spinal cord injuries during corrective surgery can occur, sometimes leading to paralysis. Here, we created three-dimensional FE models specifically matched to the spinal cords of study patients in order to examine spinal cord stress distribution during scoliosis correction surgery. These findings may help clinicians better predict the spinal segments where neurological complications could occur during surgery. Material and Methods: Such events are associated with biomechanical changes in the spinal cord during surgery, however, their underlying mechanisms are not well understood. Results: In four patients with poor prognosis, there was a concentration of stress in the spinal cord. In two patients with good prognosis, the stress distribution in the spinal cord models was uniform, and they showed no abnormal clinical manifestations postoperatively. Conclusion: This study identified a potential biomechanical mechanism of spinal cord injury caused by surgical correction of scoliosis. ## P114: Posterior trans-intervertebral osteotomy with anterior support for severe kyphotic deformity secondary to ankylosing spondylitis

Yong Hai

1,2

, Zihao Ding

1

, Yunsheng Wang

1,2

, Lijin Zhou

Beijing Chaoyang Hospital, Capital Medical University, Orthopedic Surgery, Beijing, China,

2

Center for Spinal Deformity, Capital Medical University, Beijing, China

Introduction: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is an inflammatory seronegative arthropathy affecting mainly the medial skeleton. AS causes joint pain, stiffness, and severe thoracolumbar kyphosis deformity (TKD), further restricting the patient’s daily mobility. This phenomenon frequently occurs in individuals who have reached severe stages of AS. The intensity of thoracolumbar kyphosis may diminish ambulatory capacity and compromise the ability to maintain an upright and comfortable posture. TKD exerts a discernible effect on both an individual’s physical look and functional abilities, possibly causing severe problems such as respiratory distress. The use of trans-intervertebral osteotomy as a stand-alone procedure is limited to cases of mild-to-moderate kyphotic deformities, in which the primary manifestation is compression of the anterior column. Patients with partial compression of the middle and posterior columns may not achieve satisfactory corrective outcomes using this approach. Furthermore, surgeons currently have difficulty with the increased occurrence of neurological problems resulting from direct or indirect intraoperative spinal cord injury. This study aimed to assess the efficacy of a novel spinal osteotomy technique, the posterior trans-intervertebral osteotomy with anterior support, in individuals diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis. This study utilized computer software to simulate the osteotomy procedure, predict orthopedic outcomes, and assist in preoperative planning. Results: Patients who underwent posterior trans-intervertebral osteotomy with anterior support achieved good clinical results with favorable correction rates and minimal estimated blood loss. The average preoperative and postoperative Cobb angles were 90.5° (range: 86-96°) and 43.5° (range: 34-52°), respectively. The average estimated blood loss was 500 mL (range: 300-800 mL). Patients with preoperative deficits improved their neurological status, and no complications were observed throughout the postoperative period. Conclusion: Posterior trans-intervertebral osteotomy with an anterior support procedure was performed through the intervertebral space and subsequent implantation of a cage within the transpedicular space, effectively addressing the constraints associated with the conventional trans-intervertebral osteotomy method. Our preliminary findings indicate that posterior trans-intervertebral osteotomy with anterior support is potentially more secure than the conventional method for correcting ankylosing spondylitis kyphosis.

## P115: Fusing to the sacrum or stopping short: is there a difference in outcomes among adult idiopathic scoliosis (AdIS) patients?

Christopher Mikhail

1

, Fthimnir Hassan

2

, Stephen Stephan

3

, Andrew Platt

4

2

, Joseph Lombardi

2

, Zeeshan Sardar

, Ronald A. Lehman

, Lawrence Lenke

1
Cedar Sinai Medical Center, Los Angeles, United States,

4

Introduction: Adult Spinal Deformity (ASD) is a broad category of pathology that has more recently seen increased research interest. Although numerous studies describe outcomes of surgical correction of adult spinal deformity, few studies have looked the outcomes of surgical correction of the distinct population of Adult Idiopathic Scoliosis (AdIS). The purpose of this study is to demonstrate whether AdIS patients fused to the sacrum will have inferior outcomes and more complications to those fused above the sacrum. Methods: This was a retrospective study of AdIS patients who underwent surgery with minimum 2yr follow up. SAC patients were older (55.8 ± 8.7 vs 31.1 ± 11.6, p < 0.0001), had greater EBL (1675.8 ± 683.0cc vs 914.5 ± 582.0cc, p < 0.0001), longer OR times (8.5 ± 1.1 hr vs 5.7 ± 1.9 hr, p < 0.0001) and longer LOS (7.0 ± 2.3d vs 4.1 ± 1.4d, p < 0.0001). SAC patients had larger thoracolumbar/lumbar (65.2 ± 12.3 vs 41.4 ± 15.6, p < 0.0001), lumbosacral curves (27.7 ± 9.2 vs 15.9 ± 11.3, p < 0.0001), and were more malaligned in the sagittal plane at baseline (SVA: 26.8 ± 40.3mm vs -16.8 ± 29.0, p < 0.0001). NonSAC patients, however, had a larger proximal thoracic curve (28.5 ± 14.9 vs 20.9 ± 12.8, p = 0.0337), lumbar lordosis (63.3 ± 13.5 vs 43.6 ± 16.8, p < 0.0001), and T2-T5 thoracic kyphosis (20.2 ± 11.8 vs 13.0 ± 8.3, p = 0.0044) at baseline. Both groups saw significant improvements in both radiographic parameters and in PROs at final follow up. At baseline, NonSAC presented with greater SRS22r function (4.1 ± 0.8 vs 3.7 ± 0.8, p = 0.0480), pain (3.5 ± 0.9 vs 3.0 ± 0.8, p = 0.0148), and ODI score (19.4 ± 16.9 vs 27.3 ± 14.8, p = 0.0430), NonSAC patients demonstrated a greater function score (4.6 ± 0.4 vs 4.1 ± 0.7, p = 0.0055) and lower ODI score (7.3 ± 7.6 vs 14.4 ± 13.3, p = 0.0121) at the final follow up. Despite these differences, there was no significant difference in SRS-22r total score at final follow up (SAC: 4.1 ± 0.6 vs NonSAC: 4.3 ± 0.4, p = 0.1159). No differences in intraoperative (p = 0.999) complications were observed. However, SAC patients were more likely to experience postop ileus while admitted (29.4% vs 7.9%, p = 0.0178). Although SAC patients reported greater complications between 1yr and final follow up (p = 0.0048), no difference were observed among revision rates and stratified complications (p > 0.05). Conclusions: AdIS patients treated to the SAC and NonSAC both improved radiographically and clinically with surprisingly similar SRS-22r total scores at final follow up, but NonSAC patients reporting greater function and less disability. Although SAC patients did experience more complications after 1yr, no difference in revision rates was seen.

Introduction: Surgical indications and management of Adult Idiopathic Scoliosis (AdIS) are not well defined. ## P118: Comparison of clinical and radiological outcomes of three-column lumbar osteotomies with and without interbody cages for adult spinal deformity: a database analysis

Esteban Quiceno Restrepo

1

, Mohamed Soliman

1

, Jacob Greisman

1

, Asham Khan

1

, John Pollina

1

, Jeffrey Mullin

1

1

University at Buffalo Neurosurgery, Neurosurgery, Buffalo, United States

Introduction: Correcting sagittal malalignment in adult spinal deformity (ASD) poses significant challenges. Proposed three column osteotomies, including Schwab 3 osteotomy, the “Sandwich” technique, Schwab 4 osteotomy, and Schwab 4 plus interbody cage, are aimed at achieving alignment goals. The aim of this study is to compare outcomes of three-column osteotomies with and without the use of a cage. Material and Methods: Preoperative demographic characteristics, radiographic measurements, patient-reported outcomes, complications, and fusion rates were evaluated preoperatively and at a 2-year follow-up. Three blinded, surgeons based on serial radiographs determined fusion grading. Univariate and multivariate analyses were performed to assess fusion outcomes between groups. Comparisons were made between the four-osteotomy groups and the cage and none-cage groups. Results: Patients undergoing the “Sandwich osteotomy” exhibited worse preoperative leg pain scores and lower SRS activity (p = 0.015), appearance (p = 0.007), and mental health domain scores (p = 0.0015), yet this group showed the largest mean change in the SRS mental health domain (p = 0.005). No differences in complications were found between groups (p > 0.05). Patients who underwent osteotomy with a cage were more likely to have had previous spine fusion (91.7% vs 71.4%, p = 0.010). Additionally, these patients had lower preoperative SRS mental domain scores (2.9 ± 1 vs 3.59 ± 1, p = 0.009), satisfaction scores (2.39 ± 1 vs 2.79 ± 1.2, p = 0.034), and lower preoperative SRS total scores (2.39 ± 0.6 vs 2.69 ± 0.6, p = 0.0026), but demonstrated the largest improvement in the mental health domain (0.99 ± 0.7 vs 0.39 ± 0.9, p = 0.002). The use of a cage was associated with a larger mean change in segmental lordosis at the osteotomy site (32.99 ± 9.6 vs 28.79 ± 9.5, p = 0.038). Posterolateral fusion and circumferential fusion rates were significantly higher in the cage group (79.2% vs 55.1%, p = 0.0012). Regression analysis identified the use of a cage at the osteotomy as an independent predictor for posterior fusion (OR95%3.338,CI,1.108-10.054, p = 0.032). Conclusion: While incorporating an interbody cage at contiguous disc spaces or the osteotomy site did not correlate with increased complication rates, it did show a higher incidence of posterolateral and circumferential fusion at the two-year postoperative mark and better segmental lordosis at the osteotomy site.
