## P149: Identification of risk factors for proximal junctional kyphosis following fusion from the lower thoracic spine to the pelvis through geometrical assessment

François Dantas

1

, Fatemeh Alavi

2

, Stephen Lewis

3

, Christopher J. Nielsen

3

, Raja Rampersaud

3

1
Toronto Western Hospital, Neurosurgery, Toronto, Canada,

2
University Health Network, Osteoporosis Program, Schroeder's Arthritis Institute, Toronto, Canada,

3

Toronto Western Hospital, Orthopedic Surgery, Toronto, Canada

Introduction: Proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) and failure (PJF) are recognized as common complications following adult spine deformity (ASD) surgery. Several risk factors are reported including surgical, radiographic, and patient-related factors. The multifactorial etiology of PJK and the presence of controversial risk factors highlight the necessity for ongoing research in this area. We hypothesized that commonly assessed sagittal spinopelvic parameters, along with specific geometrically defined variables derived from immediate postoperative radiographs, could clarify alignment-related risk factors for PJK. This study aimed to introduce new geometrically relevant sagittal parameters associated with PJK. Material and Methods: 91 ASD patients who underwent corrective spinal fusion from the lower thoracic spine to the pelvis were included in this single institution study. The minimum follow-up was 1 year. PJK was defined as more than 10 degrees post-to-preoperative changes in the angle between the upper endplate of the upper-instrumented vertebra (UIV) and two levels above (UIV+2). A framework was developed to automatically extract 56 sagittal alignment parameters from immediate postoperative radiographs. Among them, we defined two triangles including the femoral head (FH): fused triangle (FH_UIV_S1) and unfused triangle (FH_UIV_T1). Three geometrical parameters were defined: Gamma angle, defined as an angle between the lines connecting UIV to T1 and UIV to FH, as well as T1FH_distance, defined as the distance of UIV to a line connecting T1 to FH in the non-fused triangle. Beta angle was defined as an angle between the lines connecting UIV to FH and UIV to S1 in the fused triangle. Two-sided independent t-test was performed to determine the significant factors between PJK and non-PJK groups. Results: 42 out of 91 patients developed PJK (46%). There was no difference in sex, age, pelvic incident (PI), pelvic tilt (PT), and regional parameters such as L4_S1, L1_S1, and L1_L4 between PJK and non-PJK groups. However, 14 postoperative sagittal parameters with significant differences between the two groups were identified. Other than sagittal vertical angle (SVA), global tilt (GT), and TPA_IPPA mismatch, UIV contributed to all other 11 parameters including C2_UIV_PA, T1_UIV-pA, C2PA, TPA, UIV_L1_Cobb angle, UIV_IP_Cobb angle, UIVPA_L1PA mismatch, UIVPA_IPPA mismatch, UIV angle, Gamma, and distance to the T1_FH line. Non-PJK patients had more posteriorly inclined UIV than PJK patients (5.5o vs. 1o; p-value < 0.001). Gamma angle was larger in the non-PJK group compared to the PJK group (154o vs. 148o; p-value 0.001). Conclusion: The position of UIV following low thoracic to pelvis instrumented fusion influences the UIV inclination, Gamma angle, and distance of UIV to T1_FH line, which are important sagittal alignment variables in the geometric assessment of risk factors for PJK. Further research utilizing these methods is warranted given the association of the UIV in all but three parameters.

## P150: Machine learning-based prediction of thoracic kyphosis compensation following fusion from the lower thoracic spine to the pelvis

Christopher J. Nielsen

1

, François Dantas

2

, Fatemeh Alavi

3

, Stephen Lewis

1

, Raja Rampersaud

1

1
Toronto Western Hospital, Orthopedic Surgery, Toronto, Canada,

2
Toronto Western Hospital, Neurosurgery, Toronto, Canada,

3

University Health Network, Toronto, Canada

Introduction: Upper thoracic reciprocal change is a common compensatory mechanism following corrective fusion surgery. The upper thoracic compensatory mechanism remains poorly predictable. We hypothesized that postoperative upper thoracic parameters can be predicted by a combination of preoperative and surgical planning parameters. Thoracic kyphosis (TK) was defined as T1_UIV_Cobb angle. This study aimed to determine postoperative TK based on the preoperative and surgical planning variables in ASD patients using a machine-learning (ML) algorithm. Material and Methods: A consecutive series of patients (mean age 66.7 ± 10.8 years, 65.9% females) with ASD underwent corrective spinal fusion from the lower thoracic spine (T9-T12) to the pelvis in a single institution from 2010-2023. The preoperative and immediate postoperative radiographs were used to measure spinopelvic parameters. A predictive model using linear regression was built for postoperative PT from 91 patients (80% training, 20% validation). All extracted preoperative spinopelvic parameters and surgical parameters, such as upper-instrumented vertebra pelvic angle (UIVPA) and its distance to the sacrum, were included to build a PT predictive model. To validate the ML model, the postoperative pelvic tilt was compared with the predicted values. Results: We found that postoperative thoracic kyphosis is significantly correlated with age, four preoperative parameters, and postoperative UIVPA as a surgical planning parameter. The preoperative predictors are thoracic kyphosis, global tilt (GT), UIV tilt, and the distance of UIV to a line connecting T1 to the femoral head (FH). The ML-based model with R2 = 0.76 indicates a good correlation between predictors and postoperative TK. The mean absolute error was 5° for training and validation groups, which is within the range of measurement error. Conclusion: ML algorithm can predict postoperative compensation in the non-fused thoracic spine for patients with lower thoracic fusion to the pelvis. Leveraging this technology can be helpful for preplanning alignment to determine postoperative UIVPA and may reduce the risk of mechanical complications. This algorithm can predict changes in thoracic kyphosis in the non-instrumented spine. Important parameters based on this algorithm include patient age and global sagittal parameters, such as global tilt and UIVPA.

## P151: The usefulness of circumferential minimally invasive surgery (cMIS) using LIF and All PPS for severe adult spinal deformity

Tomohisa Harada

1,2

1
Sangubashi Spine Surgery Hospital, Tokyo, Japan,

2

Rakuwakai Marutamachi Hospital, Spine Center, Kyoto, Japan

Introduction: The purpose of this study was to investigate whether cMIS using LIF and All PPS is useful for severe ASD. Material and Methods: The subjects were 78 consecutive ASD patients (5 males and 73 females) who underwent cMIS using LIF and All PPS by a single surgeon at a single institution from October 2013 to July 2023 with at least 1 year of follow-up. The mean age at surgery for all patients was 72 years (50-84 years), and patients with bony fusion between multiple vertebrae were excluded. The range of fixation was from the lower thoracic spine to the pelvis in all cases, and the number of fixed levels was 8 in 72 cases and 9 in 6 cases. Patients with a preoperative Cobb angle or pelvic incidence (PI)-lumbar lordosis (LL) mismatch of 50 degrees or greater were classified into the severe group (S group), and those with both parameters less than 50 degrees were classified into the moderate group (M group). Preoperative and postoperative radiographic parameters (coronal Cobb angle, LL angle, PI-LL mismatch, sagittal vertical axis (SVA), operative time, intraoperative blood loss, and complications were retrospectively evaluated. Results: There were 51 patients in the S group (4 males and 47 females) and 27 patients in the M group (1 male and 26 females), with a mean age of 73 and 71 years, respectively. In the S group, the mean Cobb angle was corrected from 54 to 16 degrees, the mean LL from 4 to 50 degrees, the mean PI-LL mismatch from 48 to 0 degrees, SVA from 153 to 9 mm, and PT from 36 to 18 degrees. In the M group, the mean Cobb angle was corrected from 35 to 9 degrees, mean LL from 20 to 51 degrees, mean PI-LL mismatch from 32 to -1 degree, SVA from 84 to -5 mm, and PT from 31 to 19 degrees. Mean operative time was 378 and 346 minutes for the S and M groups, and intraoperative blood loss was 435 and 351 ml, respectively. Postoperative complications included muscle weakness and sensory disturbance of the lower extremities in 15 patients (29%) in the S group and 7 patients (about 26%) in the M group, of whom 4 patients in the S group had mild numbness and 3 patients had residual muscle weakness at the MMT3 level. Rod breakage was observed in 13 (25%) and 9 (33%) patients, respectively; PJK was observed in 3 patients in the S group and 2 patients in the M group, and 2 patients in the S group underwent revision surgery. There were also cases of postoperative iatrogenic disc herniation and intradural hematoma requiring reoperation in the S group, as well as case of intercostal artery hemorrhage requiring embolization. Conclusion: We believe that cMIS using LIF and PPS for ASD is a minimally invasive and useful technique that provides ideal correction. However, postoperative complications are frequent in patients with severely deformity, and Attention should be paid.

## P152: Does cervicothoracic flexibility affect clinical outcomes in patients undergoing multi-level posterior cervical fusions?

Devender Singh

1

, Eeric Truumees

1

, Ashley Duncan

1

, Qais Zai

1

, Matthew Geck

1

, Eva Moroz

1

, John Stokes

1

, Morgan Laviolette

1

, Vik Kohli

1

1

Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United States

Introduction: Standing multi-view X-rays and MRIs/CTs are standards of care in preoperative planning for patients undergoing cervical fusions. However, the positioning of the patient varies between the two different types of imaging. When positioned for an MRI/CT, the patient is supine, and the head is bolstered or supported. Whereas for standing X-Rays, the patient adopts their native posture and head alignment. The purpose of this study was to quantify and compare the imaging measurements between the two imaging modalities and determine if cervicothoracic flexibility had an impact on cervical alignment or clinical outcome. Materials and Methods: 227 adult patients who underwent a three or more level posterior cervical fusion were assessed. Data included demographics and radiographic measurements from both XR films and correlate measures from MRI/CT scans, surgical complications, as well as patient reported outcome measures for pain (Visual Analog Scale, VAS) and disability (Oswestry Disability Index, ODI). For each measurement technique, three cohorts were created based on distribution of the Δ between XR and MRI/CT. Results: Overall, the cohort was 53.7% female, with a mean age of 63 ± 13 years and BMI of 28.93, 44% were never smokers. The most frequently treated spinal levels were C3-C7. Median Δ T1 Slope was 9°, with a range of -1° to 45°. T1 Slope cohorts: Group I with a Δ of < 4°; Group II ≥ 4° to < 15°; Group III ≥ 15°. Significant differences between Group I and Group III existed in VAS (4.19 and 6.59, respectively) and ODI (35.4 and 45.9, respectively). For Δ C2-C7 Lordosis, the median Δ value was 4°, with a range of -11° to 44°; Group I had a Δ lordosis of < 2°; Group II ≥ 2 to < 7°; Group III ≥ 7°. Significant differences between Group I and III existed in VAS (4.6 and 6.3, respectively) and ODI (36.7 and 45.5, respectively). Median Δ C2-C7 SVA was 14.37 mm, with a range of 37.6 mm to 110.2 mm. SVA Group I had a Δ of < 7.87 mm; Group II ≥ 7.87 mm to < 27.82 mm; Group III ≥ 27.82 mm. There were significant differences between Group I and Group III in VAS (4.8 and 6.4, respectively) and ODI (34 and 45.6, respectively). Revision and complication rates positively correlated with increased Δ measurement. ANOVA analysis of the effect of age, sex, gender, BMI and smoking status on each measurement technique demonstrated age having a significant effect on Δ C2-C7 SVA. Conclusions: Larger Δ or cervical and upper thoracic flexibility between XR and MRI/CT measurements are positively correlated with higher complication and revision rates. In those patients in whom the delta between the simulated T1 slope from supine studies and the upright T1 slope was higher were found to have much greater post-operative cSVAs and reported significantly higher pain and disability scores compared to those with lower measurement Δ. Age was found to significantly impact Δ SVA measurement. Upper thoracic flexibility should be considered in selecting fusion levels and alignment goals in patients undergoing posterior cervical fusion surgery.

## P153: Association between putative neck strength, C2 slope, sagittal vertical alignment and patient reported outcomes in multi-level posterior cervical fusion - A multi center analysis

Devender Singh

1

, Eeric Truumees

, Qais Zai

, Ashley Duncan

, Eva Moroz

, Matthew Geck

, John Stokes

, Morgan Laviolette

, Vik Kohli

1

Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United States

Introduction: C2 slope, a mathematical approximation of TS-CL, may define the presence of a mismatch between cervical lordosis and thoracolumbar alignment. The change in C2 slope with active extension may be a useful of extension capacity has been used to estimate post-operative kyphosis in laminoplasty patients. We aimed to investigate the relationship between pre-operative extension capacity and clinical and radiographic outcomes in patients undergoing a three or more level posterior cervical fusion with a C7 caudal level. Our null hypothesis was that the greater pre-operative extension capacity would result in greater improvement in radiographic and patient reported outcomes. Material and Methods: Pre-operative extension capacity was measured as the change in the C2 slope (neutral vs. extension cervical x-ray films). We also collected C2 slope, cervical Sagittal Vertical Axis (cSVA), Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and Pain Visual Analog Scale (VAS). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed, and the Youden index was calculated to determine the matching C2 slope cutoff value according to the established radiographic parameter. Results: 324 patients were included in this study, with a mean age 62.6 ± 12 years, 57% female, and mean BMI of 28.7. Of these patients, 57% were non-smokers, 32.1% former-smokers and 10.9% current-smokers. The Δ C2 slope was negatively correlated with SVA (r = -0.58) and VAS and ODI. Conclusions: Neck strength, in terms of the ΔC2 slope, was positively correlated with SVA and negatively with VAS and ODI scores in patients who underwent a three or more level posterior cervical fusion. The results of this study support the hypothesis that greater extension capacity is associated with better clinical, and patient reported outcomes postoperatively. Additionally, pre- and postop C2 slope is a useful clinical prognostic factor in multilevel posterior cervical fusion.

Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United States

Introduction: The relationship between T1 Slope and Cervical Lordosis (CL), much like the relationship between Pelvic Incidence (PI) and Lumbar Lordosis (LL), serve as indicators of not only spinal alignment, but also outcomes related to overall disability and pain. ## P155: Effect of thoracic inlet angle on cervicothoracic parameters and patient reported outcomes in posterior multi-cervicothoracic fusion

Devender Singh

1

, Eeric Truumees

1

, Eva Moroz

, Qais Zai

, Ashley Duncan

, John Stokes

, Matthew Geck

1

, Morgan Laviolette

1

, Vik Kohli

1

1

Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United States

Introduction: Thoracic Inlet Angle (TIA) is created by the intersection of a line from the tip of the sternum to the midpoint of the superior T1 endplate and a line perpendicular to the superior T1 endplate. This radiographic parameter is constant and independent of posture and has been significantly correlated with cervical sagittal balance. The purpose of this study was to investigate the effect of TIA on other cervicothoracic parameters and patient reported outcomes (PROs) in patients undergoing multi-level posterior cervicothoracic fusions with a caudal end of C7, T1 or T2. Material and Methods: Retrospective, multi-center analysis of patients undergoing multilevel posterior cervicothoracic fusions terminating at C7, T1 or T2. Basic demographic data was collected, along with PROs (Oswestry Disability Index [ODI] and pain Visual Analog Scale [VAS] at intermittent intervals from preoperative to two years postoperative. Radiographic parameters (TIA, Cervical Lordosis, T1 Slope, Cervical Sagittal Vertical Alignment [cSVA]) were also measured at these intervals. Results: 257 patients were included in this analysis. Mean age was 62.6 ± 13.4 years with a mean BMI of 28.5 ± 6.6 and 68.5% female. 57% were never smokers, 32.1% were former smokers and 10.9% were current smokers. From preop to 2years postop, there was a 2.3% change in TIA, 17.2% change in cervical lordosis, 14.1% change in T1 slope and 34.9% change in cSVA. VAS and ODI saw 31.2% and 17.2% improvement, respectively, over this time frame. There was a strong positive correlation between TIA and T1 slope at both pre (r2 = 56.4) and 2 years postop (r2 = 58.4). Similar findings were observed between TIA and cSVA at pre (r2 = 58.3) and 2 years postop (r2 = 63.4). Weak positive correlations were observed between TIA and cervical lordosis, and PROs (VAS and ODI) and TIA at pre and 2 years post. Conclusions: As expected, TIA remained essentially unchanged from pre- to post-op. That said, strong positive correlations were found between TIA and T1 slope and TIA and cSVA at preoperative and 2 years postoperative. The findings of this analysis support the relationship of TIA and cervical sagittal alignment demonstrated in previous studies. Additionally, weak positive correlations between TIA and cervical lordosis and TIA and patient reported outcomes were also found. Current data suggest that surgical goals include achievement of reasonable sagittal balance. More static measures such as TIA and more potentially variable measures such as T1 slope should be considered when planning a posterior cervical reconstruction.

## P156: Impact of T1 slope-cervical lordosis discrepancy on sagittal vertical axis and patient reported outcomes following posterior cervical fusion: a multi-center retrospective analysis

Devender Singh

1

, Eeric Truumees

1

, Eva Moroz

1

, Ashley Duncan

1

, Matthew Geck

1

, John Stokes

, Morgan Laviolette

1

, Vik Kohli

1

Ascension Texas Spine and Scoliosis, Austin, United States

Introduction: The relationship between T1 slope (TS) and cervical lordosis (CL) mirrors the established correlation between pelvic incidence (PI) and lumbar lordosis (LL) in assessing spinal alignment and predicting functional outcomes in patients undergoing spinal surgeries. Understanding these parameters is crucial as they influence disability and pain outcomes post-surgery. Our null hypothesis was that there is no significant association between TS-CL discrepancy greater than 17° and Sagittal Vertical Axis (cSVA) exceeding 4 cm, nor does an cSVA > 4 cm correlate with poorer patient-reported outcomes (Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for pain and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI)). The dual purpose of this study was to- 1) Evaluate whether a TS-CL discrepancy greater than 17° predicts a cSVA greater than 4 cm in patients undergoing mutli-level posterior cervical fusion for stenosis and myelopathy, 2) investigate if an SVA > 4 cm correlates with higher patient-reported outcomes. Inclusion criteria required the surgical level to be caudal to C7 and a minimum follow-up period of two years. Data collected encompassed demographic details, radiographic measurements (T1 slope, C2-C7 CL, C2-C7 cSVA), and patient-reported outcomes (VAS, ODI). Conclusion: The findings substantiate that a TS-CL discrepancy greater than 17° is associated with an increased cSVA exceeding 4 cm in patients undergoing mutli-level posterior cervical fusion. Moreover, patients with higher SVA demonstrated poorer outcomes in terms of pain and disability, as indicated by VAS and ODI scores. These results underscore the importance of preoperative evaluation of TS-CL discrepancy to optimize surgical planning and enhance postoperative outcomes related to spinal alignment and patient-reported quality of life.

## P158: Cervical anterior arthrodesis: autologus or synthetic graft?

Eleonor José Soligo Junior

1

, Álynson Larocca Kulcheski

1

, Xavier Soler I Graells

1

, André Luís Sebben

1

, Felipe Nanni

1

, Pedro Grein

1

1

Hospital do Trabalhador, Curitiba, Brazil

Introduction: The study compares the outcomes of anterior cervical arthrodesis using either autologous iliac crest grafts or synthetic tricalcium phosphate grafts. As the population ages, degenerative cervical spine diseases become more prevalent, leading to increased spinal surgeries. Autologous iliac grafts are considered the gold standard due to their superior osseointegration and osteogenesis capabilities. However, they carry risks such as bleeding, neurological damage, and chronic pain at the donor site. To mitigate these complications, synthetic grafts, which reduce surgical time and have lower coplication risks, are explored. Material and Methods: The study involved 38 patients, aged 18 to 100, who underwent anterior cervical arthrodesis for degenerative cervical spine conditions. The patients were divided into two groups: Group 1 received autologous iliac crest grafts, and Group 2 received synthetic tricalcium phosphate grafts. Outcomes were measured using the Visual Pain Scale (VAS) and the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) at various intervals pre- and post-operation. Bone healing was assessed via CT scans nine months after surgery. Results: Mean ODI (Group 1) was 68.5% ± 4.6% preoperatively and 27.2% ± 3.8% postoperatively, being statistically relevant (p < 0.001). VAS performed to evaluate the cervical region, Group 1 pre and post-op was considered statistically relevant (p < 0.001). No significant difference was observed when comparing the mean values found in the postoperative period between Group 1 and Group 2 (p = 0.463). Only two patients complained of chronic pain, representing 10% of the total. In nine-month tomography, 100% of patients in Group 1 and 100% of Group 2 showed bone consolidation, with no statistically relevant difference (p = 0.676) between the groups. Conclusion: Similar functional and osteointegration outcomes were observed in both types of grafts. Conclusion: The study concludes that synthetic tricalcium phosphate grafts offer a viable alternative to autologous grafts, providing similar functional and osteointegration outcomes while minimizing the risks associated with autologous grafts. This makes synthetic grafts a promising option for anterior cervical arthrodesis up to two levels. Further studies could explore the potential for synthetic grafts to reduce surgical costs and improve recovery times.

## ID: 165

## P159: A rare case of cervical ligamentum flavum tophi leading to acute paraparesis: a diagnostic challenge

Rajeesh George

1

, Rohan De Silva

1

, Shuxun Lin

1

, Ishfaq Muhammad

1

1

Ng Teng Fong General Hospital, Orthopaedics, Singapore, Singapore

Background: Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by chronic hyperuricemia, leading to the deposition of monosodium urate crystals in and around joints and connective tissue (1). It is the most common crystal arthropathy with a global prevalence of 0.08%. Spinal involvement is generally believed to be uncommon (2). Tophaceous gout of the spine was first described by Kersley et al. in 1950, with a post-mortem identification in the atlas of the cervical spine leading to a forward subluxation of the atlas over the axis (3). The global burden of gout continues to increase, particularly in high-sociodemographic index (SDI) regions, with a male-to-female ratio of 3:1(4). Clinical Presentation: This case report describes a 67-year-old female with well-controlled diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and peripheral vascular disease, who presented to the emergency department with worsening upper and lower limb weakness over one week. She had no history of gout or hyperuricemia. An MRI revealed cord compression from the posterior aspect at the C4 level. Intraoperatively, chalky white deposits were noted on the ligamentum flavum at the epidural space at C4. But the Histological examination was not conclusive even though the serum uric acid levels were found to be high. Dual-energy CT also was not conclusive of gout as it was done post op. Conclusion: This case strongly suggests cervical spine involvement in gout. Clinical presentation, intraoperative findings, radiographic images, and biochemical markers collectively support this diagnosis. The lack of visible urate crystals in histology does not definitively rule out gout, especially with other supporting evidence. Pre op Dual-energy CT is a highly useful tool in the identification and management of gouty tophi. Its ability to specifically identify and quantify urate deposits, even in atypical locations, makes it an invaluable resource in both diagnosing and monitoring gout. This highlights diagnostic challenges and stresses the need for comprehensive evaluation, incorporating clinical judgment, imaging, and laboratory tests. Gout remains the most likely diagnosis, requiring appropriate management and follow-up. Future research should refine diagnostic criteria and enhance histological techniques for better detection of urate crystals in atypical cases.

## P160: Paraspinal Goutallier grade as a predictor of loss of cervical lordosis following laminoplasty

Karan Joseph

1

, Miguel Ruiz Cardozo

1

, Gabriel Trevino Verastegui

1

, Tim Bui

1

, Samuel Brehm

1

, Alexander Yahanda

1

, Magalie Cadieux

1

, Camilo Molina

1

1

Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, Neurosurgery, St. Louis, United States

Introduction: The number of operated patients that experience kyphotic deformity following cervical laminoplasty is around 10-20%. As the causes of post-laminoplasty kyphotic deformity (PKD) remain unclear, the purpose of this study was to determine whether paraspinal Goutallier grade of fat degeneration is associated with the development of this complication. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent laminoplasty for cervical myelopathy at an academic tertiary care center between January 1, 2019 and January 30, 2022. Patients were included if they underwent pre- and 1-year post-operative cervical lateral x-rays, and a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within 6 months before the index operation. PKD was defined as loss of cervical lordosis greater than -10° after measuring the difference between the pre-operative and post-operative C2-7 Cobb angle in neutral cervical lateral x-rays. Two independent reviewers who were blinded to the clinical outcome and utilized axial cuts of T2 MRI scans to perform the Goutallier classification (that grades the degree of fat degeneration) of the right and left-sided paraspinal multifidus at the C5-C6 level. The 2 sides were averaged for final Goutallier classification. To assess the association between Goutallier grades and PKD occurrence, we employed chi-square test. Results: 35 CMS patients met inclusion criteria and 4 developed PKD (11%). The cohort had a mean age of 60.31 ± 11 years old; BMI of 29.0 kg/m2 ± 6; Charlson Comorbidity Index of 2.94 ± 2. A total of 26 patients were classified as Goutallier [0-1.5) (Group 1), 6 were Goutallier [1.5-2.5) (Group 2), and 2 Goutallier [2.5-4] (Group 3). The intraclass correlation coefficient between the two raters was greater than 0.75 for the right, left-sided and averaged measures, indicating good reliability. There is a significant association at 5% significance level between averaged final Goutallier grade and occurrence of PKD after 1 year (x2 = 16.71, df = 2, p = 0.000236). Conclusion: The present study is the first to assess the association between cervical paraspinal muscle Goutallier grade and PKD. Based on our study, patients with increased cervical paraspinal degeneration may have increased risk of developing PKD complication and may benefit from tailored interventions. Some patients with increased paraspinal degeneration did not develop postoperative kyphosis, likely due to the multifactorial nature of the etiology of postoperative kyphosis.

## P161: 3D printed porous titanium cages in the treatment of cervicobrachial syndrome; clinical and radiological results of a 5-year follow-up study

Mark Arts

1

, Bart Torensma

1

, Jasper Wolfs

1

1

Haaglanden Medical Center, The Hague, Netherlands

Background: 3D-printed titanium has been introduced as an alternative implant technology for anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) using an interbody cage. The porous titanium cage design is intended to facilitate spinal fusion, but the contemporary scientific literature lacks conclusive long-term clinical and radiological data. We assessed the long-term clinical and radiological outcome of 3-D printed porous titanium cervical cages. Methods: We recruited 34 out of 49 patients previously enrolled in the EFFECT trial on 3D printed titanium cages, for 5 years follow-up. Objectives were the evaluation of Neck Disability Index, Visual Analog Scale of arm pain and neck pain, Likert self-reported perceived recovery, EQ-5D, fusion status, and subsidence. Fusion was defined as rotation ≤ 4° and ≤ 1.25 mm translation at the index level, using flexion-extension radiograph. Results: All patients had good outcomes in terms of NDI (12.5 ± 15.4), VAS neck pain (23.5 ± 24.1), VAS arm pain (18.7 ± 20.2), and EuroQol (0.77 ± 0.24). 88.6% of the patients experienced complete or nearly complete recovery. NDI improved significantly at 5 years compared to 1 year, all other outcome measures did not significantly differ from the 12 months results. The fusion rate at the index level increased from 91.5% at 12 months to 100% at 5 years. Conclusions: 3D printed stand-alone porous titanium cervical implants are effective in terms of clinical and radiological outcome with 88.6% complete or nearly complete recovery, and fusion rate of 100% at 5 years follow-up. Moreover, solid single level anterior cervical fusion can be achieved without additional plating.

## P163: Signal change in cervical spondylotic myelopathy as a marker of neurological prognosis

Isabelle Stockman

1

, Esteban Quiceno Restrepo

2

, Mohamed Soliman

2

, Benjamin Ciocca

1

, Ethan Herbold

1

, Ryan Goliber

1

, Charles Stube

1

, Deanna Chan

1

, Shashwat Shah

1

, Hendrick Francois

1

, Benard Okai

1

, Asham Khan

2

, John Pollina

2

, Jeffrey Mullin

2

1
Jacobs School of Medicine And Biomedical Sciences, Neurosurgery, Buffalo, United States,

2

University at Buffalo Neurosurgery, Neurosurgery, Buffalo, United States

Introduction: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy can lead to severe functional consequences for patients. Predicting the final clinical condition following surgical intervention and understanding the factors that influence recovery or permanent neurological deficits are crucial for counseling patients and their families. The objective of our study was to identify preoperative radiographic and prognostic factors that can predict the final neurological outcome in patients with cervical spondylotic myelopathy who are undergoing cervical fusion. Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted on consecutive patients with cervical spondylotic myelopathy who underwent cervical spine surgery for decompression and stabilization. The inclusion criteria comprised adult patients over 18 years old with preoperative cervical MRI and a postoperative follow-up of at least 12 months. All radiographic parameters were evaluated on the preoperative MRI, including the T1 and T2 signal intensity within the myelopathy area of the spinal cord, the anteroposterior and transverse diameter of the spinal canal, and the signal intensity of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Preoperative and postoperative clinical outcomes were assessed using the modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score. Results: The study included a total of 43 patients. When patients were categorized based on their final mJOA score, with a score equal to or higher than 16 versus a score lower than 16, significant differences were observed between the groups in terms of the intensity of signal change on the spinal cord T2 sequences relative to the intensity of the CSF in the same T2 sequence preoperatively(p=0.008), AP spinal canal diameter (p = 0.028). No other differences were found between the groups in the univariate analysis. A multivariate regression analysis examining the association of preoperative imaging variables with mJOA (modified Japanese Orthopedic Association) scores, only the T1 Mean variable was found to have a statistically significant relationship with mJOA (p = 0.041). Conclusion: These findings indicate that although certain preoperative MRI measures are associated with mJOA scores, their predictive value differs. Notably, T1 Mean emerged as a significant predictor. Additional research is required to develop a standardized index for predicting postoperative outcomes.

## P164: Surgery in cervical spondylotic myelopathy: should we do it or not?

Shah Alam

1

, Md. Ziaul Hasan

2

, Sarwar Jahan

2

, Abdullah Al Mamun

2

1
Bangladesh Spine and Orthopedic Hospital, BSOH, Spine and Orthopedic Surgery, Dhaka, Bangladesh,

2

National Institute of Traumatology and Orthopedic Rehabilitation, NITOR, Spine and Orthopedic Surgery, Dhaka, Bangladesh

Introduction: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy (CSM) is the most common cause of spinal dysfunction in the elderly. Operative management is beneficial for most patients with moderate/severe myelopathy. This study examines the potential confounding effects of age, sex, duration of symptoms, and comorbidities on the functional outcomes and postoperative complications in patients who underwent cervical decompressive surgery. Methods: We included 48 patients who underwent surgery from December 2015 to October 2023. Functional outcomes were assessed using the Nurick grading system and the modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association. 17 patients operated by ACDF, 10 ACCF and 21 posterior surgery by laminectomy and lateral mass screw fixation. Results: There were 29 men and 19 women with a mean age of 57 years (range 32-88 years). The mean duration of symptoms was 25.2 months (range 1-120 months). There was a significant functional recovery from baseline to 6 months after surgery (p < 0.01). Postoperative complications occurred in 18.5% of cases. Although the occurrence of complications was not significantly associated with sex (p = 0.188), number of ICD-9 codes (p = 0.113), duration of symptoms (p = 0.309), surgical approach (p = 0.248), or number of spine levels treated (p = 0.454), logistic regression analysis showed that patients who developed complications were significantly older than patients who had no complications (p = 0.018). Post operative NDI and modified JOA score was improved significantly (p ≤ 0.01). Conclusions: Our results indicate that surgery for CSM is associated with significant functional recovery. Age is a potential predictor of complications after decompressive surgery for CSM. Whereas older patients with a greater number of pre-existing medical comorbidities had less favorable functional outcomes after surgery.

## P165: Complications of anterior cervical spine surgery: our center’s 2-year experience

Rute Santos Pereira

1

, João Cruz

1

, Joana Rodrigues

1

, André Cunha

1

, Ricardo Simoes

1

1

Hospital do Divino Espírito Santo, Orthopedics, Ponta Delgada, Portugal

Introduction: The anterior approach to the cervical spine is widely used for a variety of clinical conditions. Complications differ from those of the posterior approach due to the unique anatomy of the anterior aspect of the neck and have their own peculiarities. Material and Methods: Data were retrospectively collected on all patients with degenerative pathology who underwent anterior cervical spine surgery (excluding trauma, infection, and tumor) by the same surgeon between the years 2021-2023 regarding demographics, pathology, surgery, levels, operative time, neuromonitoring, hours to discharge, intraoperative and postoperative complications - minimum 3-month follow-up (immediate, consultation referral, or emergency department visit within 1 month). Results: We obtained 30 patients who underwent surgery during the mentioned period. Of all patients, 63% (N = 19) were female and the pathologies in order of frequency were Herniated disc (HD) with foraminal and/or central compression, cervical spondylotic myelopathy (CSM), cervical instability and acute spinal cord compression syndrome. The approach was systematic: right transverse, with microscope and image intensifier support. The most common procedure was cervical arthrodesis (n = 22), followed by disc arthroplasty (n = 8). The most commonly operated level was C5-C6 (N = 23). The average operative time was 1h46 for 1 level (N = 14), 2h26 for 2 levels (N = 13) and 2h35 for 3 levels (N = 3). The average length of stay after surgery was 42.4 hours (34.6 hours if patients coming from other islands or requiring FT inpatient were excluded). The complication rate was 20% (N = 6): 6.6% left C5 paresis (N = 2, both in patients with MEC and C4-C5 level approach), 3.3% dural injury (N = 1), 3.3% dysphagia (N = 1), 3.3% dysphonia (N = 1), and 3.3% ER visit for postoperative complaints (N = 1). With the exception of one patient with C5 paresis, all had complete resolution of the complaints related to the complications. Conclusion: Morbidity in anterior spinal surgery is low, but it has unique characteristics, particularly in relation to nerve, vascular, aero-digestive and bone structures. The limitations of our study were its retrospective nature, the size of the sample and the lack of evaluation scales. Our aim is to raise awareness of the most frequent complications of this type of surgery, which, although important, usually resolve completely.

## P166: Tranexamic acid use is associated with new-onset arrhythmia following cervical spine surgery

Robert Oris

1

, Jonathan Dalton

1

, Rajkishen Narayanan

1

, Omar Tarawneh

1

, Michael Carter

1

, Mengyi Sun

1

, Marco Goldberg

1

, Allison Toth

1

, Rachel Huang

1

, Jarod Olson

1

, Chloe Herczeg

1

, Joydeep Baidya

1

, Jose Canseco

1

, Alan Hilibrand

1

, Alex Vaccaro

1

, Gregory Schroeder

1

, Chris Kepler

1

1

Rothman Orthopaedics, Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) and posterior cervical discectomy and fusion (PCDF) are common procedures performed to treat degenerative diseases of the cervical spine. Due to decreased healthcare costs and comparable outcomes to those performed in the inpatient setting, cervical spine surgeries are increasingly being performed in the outpatient setting. Despite these advantages, up to 6% of patients initially treated outpatient basis require transfer to an inpatient hospital. Prior work suggests that 20%-35% of transfers after spinal surgeries were due to an arrhythmia, a condition that is associated with increased morbidity, mortality, length of stay, readmissions, and cost. Identifying patients at high risk for developing new-onset arrhythmias after cervical spine surgery is therefore important. However, existing literature on associated risk factors is lacking. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to identify patient-specific factors that place patients at increased risk for new-onset arrhythmia following cervical spine surgery. Methods: This is an IRB-approved retrospective cohort study of patients > 18 years who underwent elective 1-4 level ACDF, PCDF, or combined ACDF/PCDF at an academic tertiary care center between 2014-2022. Demographic characteristics including age, sex, body mass index, insurance status, and socioeconomic status as assessed by the distressed community index (DCI) were collected. A manual review of electronic medical records (EMR) was performed to record the number of levels fused, inpatient complications, and to confirm the patient had an inpatient arrhythmia. Arrhythmias were considered for inclusion if the patient had no prior documented history of arrhythmia, and if the arrhythmia required a cardiology consultation. Surgeries performed in the setting of trauma, infection, or tumor were excluded. Patients were propensity-matched in a 3:1 fashion based on procedure type and levels. Outcomes assessed included 30 and 90-day readmissions and reoperations. Multivariate linear regression analysis was performed to assess independent predictors of new-onset arrhythmia. Results: In total, 124 patients were included (93 without arrhythmia, 31 with arrhythmia). No significant differences were observed in mean age, body mass index (BMI), Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), or past medical history (p > 0.05). A significantly higher proportion of patients with arrhythmias were smokers compared to those without arrhythmias (58.1% vs 14.0%, p < 0.001). Mean levels fused, total administered intraoperative fluids, estimated blood loss, and mean volume of cell saver used were comparable across both groups. Intraoperatively, a significantly higher proportion of patients who developed arrhythmia received TXA (25.8% vs. 5.38%, p = 0.003). 90-day readmissions were significantly higher in the arrhythmia group compared to the no arrhythmia group (29% vs 10.8%, p = 0.021). However, 30-day readmissions and 1-year reoperations were similar between groups. On regression analysis, TXA was identified as a significant predictor of arrhythmia development postoperatively (odds ratio = 6.22, p = 0.004). Conclusion: In our propensity-matched analysis, we identified TXA as an independent predictor for new-onset arrhythmia postoperatively following cervical spine surgery. Clinicians should be advised of this unique finding, and further large-scale confirmatory investigations are needed.

## P167: Recovery trajectories following anterior versus posterior fusion surgery for cervical degenerative pathology

Katie Lee

1

, Arpitha Pamula

1

, Christopher Lloyd

1

, Alex Tang

2

, Tan Chen

3

1
Geisinger Commonwealth School of Medicine, Scranton, United States,

2
Geisinger Health, Orthopaedic Surgery Northeast Residency, Wilkes-Barre, United States,

3

Geisinger Health, Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Wilkes-Barre, United States

Introduction: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) and posterior cervical decompression and instrumented fusion (PDIF) are two common spinal procedures for treating cervical degenerative pathology. While previous studies have compared outcomes and complication profiles between ACDF and PDIF, there is limited outcomes data investigating the rates and trajectory of clinical improvement between the two techniques. The purpose of this study was to (1) compare trends in patient reported neck disability index (NDI) scores perioperatively, (2) identify demographic and perioperative characteristics that may influence rate of improvement, and (3) compare surgical complication and reoperation rates. Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis was performed from 2019–2023 identifying patients who underwent elective ACDF or PDIF for cervical degenerative disease. Data collected included patient demographics, diagnosis, perioperative data, surgical complications and reoperations, number of fusion levels, and longitudinal NDI scores. Delta (∆) NDI was calculated as the difference between the present NDI score from the preoperative NDI at each timepoint. A minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of 11 was assumed based on previous literature. Descriptive and inferential statistics were performed. Results: A total of 309 patients (ACDF, n = 271; PDIF n = 38) were included. Average follow-up time was 2.2 years. The ACDF cohort was younger (56.1 vs. 60.4, p = 0.016), had a greater proportion of primary surgeries compared to revisions (99% vs. 74%, p < 0.0001), lower estimated blood loss (34.9 ml vs. 128.2 ml, p = 0.0001), and shorter length of stay (2.0 days vs. 2.9 days, p = 0.001). No differences were found between the number of fusion levels, complications or revision rates. The ACDF cohort had significantly lower NDI scores than the PDIF cohort at all timepoints (p < 0.0001) and greater ∆NDI at latest follow-up (-24.1 ± 16.9 vs. -15.9 ± 17.7, p = 0.006). At 3-months, 72% of ACDF patients achieved MCID versus 46% PCF patients (p = 0.004). At 6-months, 76% of ACDF patients achieved MCID versus 50% PCF patients (p = 0.005). At 1-year, 78% of ACDF patients achieved MCID versus 61% PCF patients (p = 0.04). Subgroup analysis was performed for radiculopathy, myelopathy, and myeloradiculopathy diagnoses at different timepoints with no statistically significant difference between these diagnoses at all time points 6-week, 12-week, 6-month, 1-year (p = 0.107, p = 0.697, p = 0.523, p = 0.397). Analysis of single-level and multi-level fusion cohorts also demonstrated similar long-term improvement exceeding MCID (71% single-level vs. 79% multi-level, p = 0.126). No demographic or perioperative factor was found to influence ∆NDI scores based on multivariate linear regression analysis. Conclusion: Both patients undergoing ACDF or PDIF for cervical degenerative pathologies achieve long term clinical improvement exceeding MCID with similar complication rates. The ACDF cohort demonstrated a more rapid postoperative recovery, with a significantly greater proportion of patients achieving MCID by 3 months than the PDIF cohort. At 1 year postoperatively, a greater proportion of anterior procedures achieved MCID. Clinical improvement was similar regardless of diagnoses of radiculopathy, myelopathy, or myeloradiculopathy. There are also no differences in long term NDI improvement between single and multi-level procedures. Our results provide guidance in preoperative counseling, establishing realistic recovery timelines, and managing postoperative expectations.

## P168: Fatty infiltration of the multifidus muscles is associated with loss of cervical lordosis after cervical laminoplasty

Karan Joseph

1

, Miguel Ruiz Cardozo

1

, Gabriel Trevino Verastegui

1

, Tim Bui

1

, Samuel Brehm

1

, Alexander Yahanda

1

, Magalie Cadieux

1

, Camilo Molina

1

1

Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, Neurosurgery, St. Louis, United States

Introduction: Sarcopenia is the gradual loss of muscle mass and strength and is considered a manifestation of frailty. Sarcopenia has been demonstrated to be associated with adverse postoperative events in spinal patients, however its role in postoperative kyphotic deformities is unknown. Our study aims to use a quantitative method to assess the degree of sarcopenia in the paraspinal musculature and evaluate the relationship between the extent of sarcopenia and postoperative kyphotic deformity (PKD) in cervical laminoplasty patients. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent laminoplasty for cervical myelopathy at an academic tertiary care center between January 1, 2019 and January 30, 2022. Patients were included if they underwent pre- and 1-year post-operative cervical lateral x-rays, and a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within 6 months before the index operation. PKD was defined as loss of cervical lordosis greater than −10° after measuring the difference between the pre-operative and post-operative C2-7 Cobb angle in neutral cervical lateral x-rays. The degree of muscle fat infiltration in the paraspinal muscles was assessed qualitatively using the Goutallier classification and quantitatively by manual segmentation and thresholding of the fatty voxels. Chi-square and Mann-Whitney test analyses were performed where appropriate. Optimal fat cutoff determination was calculated using maximally selected rank statistics. Results: 35 patients were included in the study. The mean age of the cohort was 60.2 ± 11 years. The mean BMI of the cohort was 29.4 ± 6. The mean Charlson Comorbidity Index for the cohort was 3.1 ± 3. 4 patients were found to have post-operative kyphosis. Qualitatively, a total of 27 patients were classified as Goutallier [0-1.5) (Group 1), 6 were Goutallier [1.5-2.5) (Group 2), and 2 Goutallier [2.5-4] (Group 3). There is a significant association between averaged final Goutallier grade and occurrence of PKD after 1 year (p = 0.0002). Quantitatively, the average fatty infiltration percentage for the kyphotic patients was 19.8% ± 7% vs 12.9% ± 9% for non-kyphotic patients. After excluding outliers, a significant association was found between the percentage of fatty infiltration and the PKD after 1 year (p-value = 0.02). Optimal fat cutoff between kyphotic vs non-kyphotic patients was 12.9% (p = 0.07). Conclusion: The present study demonstrated that, with outliers excluded, patients with higher degree of fatty infiltration were associated with PKD. Based on our results, patients with increased cervical paraspinal degeneration may have increased risk of developing PKD. With this information, surgeons may be better equipped to predict a patient’s postoperative risk for PKD.

## P169: Efficacy, safety and reliability of the single anterior approach for sub-axial cervical spine dislocation

Sharif Ahmed Jonayed

1

1

National Institute of Traumatology and Orthopaedic Rehabilitation, NITOR, Spine Surgery, Dhaka, Bangladesh

Background: Though there is ongoing controversy regarding the best treatment option for cervical spine dislocation (CSD), anterior cervical surgery with direct decompression is becoming widely accepted. However, managing all cases of sub axial CSD entirely by a single anterior approach is rarely seen in the published literature. Methods: The study comprised patients with sub axial CSD who underwent surgical stabilization utilizing a single anterior approach. Most of the CSD was reduced and anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) were performed. Anterior cervical corpectomy and fusion (ACCF) were done in unreduced dislocations. The patient's neurological condition, radiological findings, and functional outcomes were assessed. SPSS version 25.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY) was used for statistical analysis. Results: The total number of operated cases was 64, with an average of 42 months of follow-up. The mean age was 34.50 ± 11.92 years. The most prevalent level of injury was C5/C6 (57.7%). Reduction was achieved in 92.2% of cases; only 7.8% of patients needed corpectomy. The typical operative time was 84.25 ± 9.55 minutes, with an average blood loss of 112.12 ± 25.27 ml. All cases except complete spinal cord injury (CSI) were improved neurologically (87.63%). The mean Neck Disability Index (NDI) was 11.14 ± 11.43, and the pre-operative mean visual analog score (VAS) was finally improved to 2.05 ± 0.98 (p < 0.05). In all cases, fusion was achieved. The most common complication was transient dysphagia (23.4%). After surgery, no patient developed or aggravated a neurological impairment. Implant failure was not observed at the final follow-up except for two cases where screws were pulled out partially. Conclusion: Based on the results of this study, a single anterior approach is a safe and effective procedure for sub axial CSD treatment with favorable radiological, neurological, and functional outcomes.
Keywords: Traumatic cervical spine injury, anterior cervical corpectomy and fusion (ACCF), sub axial cervical spine dislocation (CSD), anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF), single anterior approach

## P170: Laminoplasty with foraminotomy versus anterior cervical discectomy and fusion for cervical myeloradiculopathy

Dong-Ho Lee

1

, Sehan Park

1

, Chang Ju Hwang

1

, Jae Hwan Cho

1

1

Asan Medical Center, Seoul, Souh Korea

Introduction: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) combined with uncinate process resection and laminoplasty combined with foraminotomy (LPF) have been used to perform cervical cord and root decompression in patients with combined cervical myelopathy and radiculopathy (CMR). The present study was conducted to compare the clinical and radiographic outcomes of ACDF with those of LPF for the treatment of CMR. Methods: Patients with CMR who underwent ACDF or LPF and were followed up for at least 2 years were retrospectively reviewed. C2–C7 lordosis, C2–C7 sagittal vertical axis, and cervical lordosis was determined. The visual analog scale (VAS) scores for neck and arm pain, neck disability index (NDI), and Japanese Orthopedic Association (JOA) scores were analyzed. The radiographic and clinical outcomes of the two groups were compared. Results: Eighty-four patients each were included in the ACDF and LPF groups (n = 42 in each group) after the application of the inclusion criteria and propensity score matching. A significant decrease in C2–C7 lordosis (p < 0.001) and cervical range of motion (ROM; p < 0.001) was observed in the LPF and ACDF groups, respectively. A significant increase in the neck pain VAS score (p < 0.001) and NDI (p < 0.001) was observed in the ACDF group. No significant increase in the neck pain VAS score was observed in the LPF group (p = 0.103). The neck pain VAS score (p = 0.026) and NDI (p = 0.021) in the LPF group were significantly greater than those in the ACDF group at 6 months postoperatively. The arm pain VAS and JOA scores showed significant improvement in the LPF (p = 0.003 and 0.043, respectively) and ACDF (p < 0.001 and 0.039, respectively) groups. The postoperative results did not differ significantly between the two groups. Conclusion: LPF and ACDF yielded similar outcomes for arm pain and neurological recovery. However, greater postoperative neck pain and postoperative loss of lordosis were observed in the LPF group, whereas early significant improvement in neck pain and decreased postoperative ROM were observed in the ACDF group.

## P171: Trends for cervical laminoplasty in Medicare beneficiaries of the United States of America

Pouya Alijanipour

1

, Remington Crossnoe

1

, James Glover

1

1

University of Texas Medical Branch, Orthopedic Surgery and Rehabilitation, Galveston, United States

Introduction: Cervical laminoplasty is widely performed as an effective surgical decompression for treatment of multilevel cervical stenosis and myelopathy. This study aims to investigate recent trends in the utilization of laminoplasty by orthopedic and neuro-surgeons within the Medicare population in the United States of America. Material and Methods: Utilizing data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, between 2012 and 2022, all claims associated with laminoplasty were identified (Current Procedural Terminology [CPT] code: 63051). The results were further categorized based on primary surgical specialty (orthopedics versus neurosurgery). Results: A total of 4,317 laminoplasty surgeries were identified between 2012 and 2022. Laminoplasty interventions increased from 10.1 to 12.8 procedures per 1 million Medicare enrollees, reflecting a 27% increase. Both orthopedic and neurosurgeons experienced a significant increase in laminoplasty utilization, with a 42% and 12% increase, respectively. Orthopedic surgeons performed consistently more laminoplasty procedures compared to neurosurgeons (54% vs 46%, p < 0.001). Laminoplasty constituted 9.2% of total posterior cervical decompression surgeries performed by orthopedic surgeons versus 5.3% for neurosurgeons (p < 0.001). Conclusion: Between 2012 and 2022, there has been a notable increase in laminoplasty procedures in US Medicare population. While orthopedic and neurosurgeons have a relatively split procedure share, recent trends indicate consistent difference in the utilization of cervical laminoplasty procedure by these specialties.

Introduction: Currently, in the specialized literature there are no substantiated clinical and radiological indications for differentiated use of Anterior Cervical Discectomy and Fusion (ACDF) and Anterior Cervical Corpectomy and Fusion (ACCF) in the treatment of patients with two-segmental cervical degenerative diseases. ## P173: Translation, cultural adaptation and validation of the Nurick scale into Portuguese

Guilherme Pajanoti

1

, Lucas Seabra Fernandes

1

, Julia Martins De Oliveira

1

, Brenand Asfora

1

, Nelson Astur

1

, Mario Lenza

1

, Eliane Antonioli

1

, Pedro Pohl

1

1

Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein, Sao Paulo, Brazil

Introduction: Degenerative cervical myelopathy stands as the primary non-traumatic cause of spinal cord dysfunction in adults. Neurological assessment tools rooted in functionality, such as the Nurick scale and the Japanese Orthopaedic Association Score (JOA), are commonly employed. The latter was revised and culturally adapted to Western norms by Chiles et al. in 1999, resulting in the modified JOA score (mJOA). The objective of this study is to translate, cross-culturally validate, and assess the reproducibility of the Nurick scale into Brazilian Portuguese among patients with cervical degenerative myelopathy. Material and Methods: The translation of the Nurick scale was carried out following the methodology proposed by Beaton et al. This study comprised two phases: initial translation, back-translation, final version assessment, and application test evaluation. In total, 70 patients were evaluated, 36 of whom belonged to the group of patients with cervical myelopathy and 34 to the control group. At this stage, the scale was applied to 10 patients, 5 with myelopathy and 5 in the control group. The examiners then responded whether or not they understood each item and commented discursively, and when two or more examiners did not understand a particular item, it was reformulated until the final version of NURICK – BRASIL was obtained. Next, the mJOA and the final version of NURICK-BRAZIL were applied to both groups, and data were collected. Data analysis was performed, and variables were described using mean, standard deviation, median, interquartile range (1st and 3rd quartiles), and minimum and maximum values. The difference between the measurements in the control group and those in the patients was compared using Mann-Whitney tests. The relationship between the Nurick and mJOA scales was measured by Spearman’s correlation. Analyses were performed using the R statistical package, and the significance level adopted was 5%. Results: Mann-Whitney comparison tests revealed significant differences in the NURICK-BRAZIL scale between the control and patient groups. Spearman's correlation coefficient indicated a robust negative correlation between the NURICK-BRAZIL and mJOA scales. These findings suggest that the adapted Nurick scale in Brazilian Portuguese (NURICK-BRAZIL) holds potential for validation in evaluating patients with degenerative cervical myelopathy. Conclusion: The translation, adaptation, and validation of the original Nurick scale in Brazilian Portuguese (NURICK-BRAZIL) demonstrate similarity, applicability, good comprehension, and significant potential for widespread utilization as a valuable clinical and scientific evaluation tool for cervical myelopathy patients.

The average JOA score was 7.08 ± 2.64 ranging from 1 to 11 showing that the majority of patients recovered. Better clinical results were obtained in most of the cases. Conclusion: Cental laminectomy and lateral mass screw fixation in multilevel degenerative spondylotic myelopathy are safe and effective procedures with good to excellent results.

## P175: Influence of subsidence after stand-alone anterior cervical disectomy and fusion in patients with degenerative cervical disease: a long-term follow-up study

Jung-Kil Lee

1

, Seong-Chan Jung

1

, Jiho Jung

1

, Jong-Hwan Hong

1

, Moon-Soo Han

1

1

Chonnam National University Hospital and Medical School, Neurosurgery, Gwang-ju City, Souh Korea

Introduction: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) with plate fixation is commonly recommended for degenerative cervical disease. Concerns about costs and complications, such as screw failure and dysphagia, have led to the exploration of stand-alone ACDF without plates, but most studies have limited follow-ups to ≤ 2 years. A significant challenge in stand-alone ACDF is subsidence (19-63%), leading to cervical kyphotic changes or clinical deterioration. Studies comparing stand-alone ACDF with plate fixation show conflicting results. This study aims to address the lack of long-term research by evaluating subsidence's impact in stand-alone ACDF with polyether ether ketone (PEEK) cages and no plate fixation, analyzing both clinical and radiological outcomes over an extended period. Material and Methods: This retrospective study enrolled 53 patients with 79 segments with degenerative cervical disease treated with stand-alone ACDF with ≥ 5 years of follow-up. Segmental angle (SA), cervical sagittal alignment (CSA), subsidence, and fusion were analyzed. Visual analog scale (VAS) scores and neck disability index (NDI) were also evaluated. Subsidence occurred in 24 (45.2%) patients and 38 segments (48.1%) at the last follow-up. Results: The mean VAS score and NDI had improved in both the subsidence and non- subsidence groups. The mean SA at the last follow-up had increased to 1.3° ± 8.5° in the subsidence group and to 1.5° ± 5.2° in the non-subsidence group compared with the post-operative SA (p < .001). The overall mean CSA at the last follow-up increased over time in both the groups compared with the post-operative CSA (p = .003). The fusion rate at 1 year after surgery was 86.8% and 82.9% in the subsidence and non-subsidence groups, respectively. However, the differences in the SA, CSA, and fusion rates between the groups were not statistically significant (p = .117, .98, and .682, respectively). Conclusion: Subsidence after stand-alone ACDF occurs to a certain capacity; however, it does not appear to significantly influence the radiological and clinical outcomes if foramen decompression is adequately and sufficiently provided in a long-term follow-up study. In contrast, subsidence appears to positively affect the fusion rate in the short-term follow-up.

, Andrei Kalinin

, Viktor Karavaev

, K. Daniel Riew

Irkutsk State Medical Academy of Postgraduate Education, Traumatology, Orthopedic and Neurosurgery, Irkutsk, Russian Federation,

Railway Clinical Hospital, Neurosurgery, Irkutsk, Russian Federation,

4
Kazakhstan-Russian Medical University, Neurosurgery, Almaty, Kazakhstan,

5
Asfendiyarov Kazakh National Medical University, Neurosurgery, Almaty, Kazakhstan,

6
Columbia University, Orthopedic Surgery, New York, United States,

7

Weill Cornell Medical Schoo, Neurological Surgery, New York, United States

Introduction: Double Crush Syndrome is a rarely diagnosed condition and can be one of the causes of negative treatment outcomes following cervical spine surgery. Currently, choosing the optimal diagnostic and therapeutic modalities in treating patients with double crush syndrome remains unresolved. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the results of surgical treatment in patients with double crush syndrome associated with cervical radiculopathy and upper limb peripheral nerve compression after staged and simultaneous operations. Material and Methods: The study included 79 patients with double crush syndrome (cervical radiculopathy and syndrome of Guyon’s canal or Carpal tunnel syndrome). At Last Follow-up, an intra-group analysis revealed comparable clinical effectiveness according to clinical scales (p > 0.05). Conclusion: Our data suggests that double crush syndrome is not an uncommon finding and surgeons are advised to consider it as a possibility in anyone with neurologic symptoms. ## P178: Indications for surgery in the treatment of Parkinson's disease: a descriptive study

Henri-Arthur Leroy

1,2

, Pierre De Buck

3

, Tuong LU

1

, Boulos Ghannam

1

, Pierre Haettel

1

, Richard Assaker

1,4

1
CHU Lille, Department of Neurosurgery, Lille, France,

2
AO Spine, Chairman for France, Davos, Switzerland,

3
Institut Catholique de Lille, Faculté de Médecine, Maïeutique, Sciences de la Santé, Lille, France,

4

AO Spine, Minimally Invasive Task Force, Davos, Switzerland

Study Design: Observational Descriptive Study + Illustrative Case. Introduction: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative condition affecting more than eight million people worldwide. Over the years, severe spine deformities can appear and influence the patient's quality of life, including autonomy, professional activities, social contact, and self-image. When non-surgical treatments fail, spine surgery becomes the last and ultimate option to restore spinal balance and improve the patient's quality of life. Spine surgery in patients with PD is a challenging condition, requiring multidisciplinary care between surgeon, rheumatologist, neurologist, and geriatrician. High rates of rod breakage, pseudoarthrosis, and persistent sagittal imbalance have been reported. The primary objective of our analysis is to improve the selection criteria for surgical intervention in PD patients with severe spinal deformities after the failure of non-surgical treatment options. Our cohort also aims at highlighting the reasons for surgical adverse events and complications. Material and Methods: Herein, we depict a large single-center cohort based on 5786 patients operated on for spine for the first time. We used our national health insurance database (PMSI) to identify individuals operated on in the Department of Neurosurgery (Lille University Hospital) between 2016 and 2022. Inclusion criteria were: 1- patient’s file including one or more keywords related to spine surgery, 2 - operated in the neurosurgery OR and 3- patient’s file featuring the necessary information about drugs and events during intraoperative time. Over 7 years, we identified 63 patients with PD. An algorithm was then used to analyze our institutional health database and to list the different surgeries realized according to the surgical reports. They were classified according to their risk of intraoperative bleeding: low, variable, or important. In the same way, the materials and instrumentation used during the surgery were extracted from surgical reports to stratify the type of intervention: invasive or mini-invasive technique. Results: PD patients were overrepresented compared to the general population, with a prevalence of 1.1%. The risk of surgical bleeding in PD patients was distributed as follows: low bleeding 55% (n = 30), variable bleeding 31% (n = 17), and important bleeding 15% (n = 8). Regarding surgery technique, mini-invasive instrumentations were used in 45% of surgeries in PD patients (n = 26), and not used in 55% (n = 32) of them. From the 63 patients who presented with PD, the surgical revision rate at one year was 14.3% (n = 9). Conclusion: Parkinson’s disease patients can experience complex overall sagittal spine imbalance. In rare case, spine surgery is the last treatment option. However, this ultimate alternative requires a global approach, involving multidisciplinary care. We advocate that each patient must benefit from personalized decision-making, to anticipate adverse events and respect the spine balance parameters when surgical corrections are necessary. This must be done after failure of all non-surgical treatment alternatives. Due to the complexity of the cases, minimally invasive surgery should be preferred whenever possible, under the supervision of at least two senior surgeons.

## P180: Patient risk factors associated with extended length of stay and 90-day hospital readmissions following posterior cervical decompression and fusion

Joydeep Baidya

1

, Jonathan Dalton

1

, Olivia Opara

1

, Rajkishen Narayanan

1

, Jarod Olson

1

, Robert Oris

1

, Michael Carter

1

, Bergin Brown

1

, Allison Toth

1

, Waqaas Hassan

1

, Gokul Karthikeyan

1

, Eric Teichner

1

, Jose Canseco

1

, Alan Hilibrand

1

, Alex Vaccaro

1

, Gregory Schroeder

1

, Chris Kepler

1

1

Rothman Orthopaedic Institute, Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: Posterior cervical decompression and fusion (PCDF) is used for a wide range of degenerative cervical disease, and can have significant complication risk including C5 palsy, infection, and delayed wound healing. These adverse events can cause increased hospital stay (LOS) or readmission. PCDF has been associated with longer length of stay/readmission compared to other cervical fusion procedures. However, no study has identified specific risk factors for these complications. This study aims to elucidate factors predictive of prolonged LOS and readmissions to improve preoperative counseling/optimization and postoperative care. Material and Methods: Adult patients who underwent PCDF for cervical myelopathy, radiculopathy, or myeloradiculopathy at a tertiary care center (2017-2022) were retrospectively identified using CPT codes 22612 and 22630. Those with combined anterior-posterior approach or surgery for trauma, tumor, or infection were excluded. Patients were stratified into two groups based on LOS > 2 or < 2 days, and on whether they were readmitted within 90 days postoperatively. Demographic and surgical characteristics were compared between groups using univariate analysis for association with LOS and readmission. Factors significant on univariate analysis were assessed with multivariate regression. Alpha was set at 0.05. Results: 378 patients met inclusion criteria. For LOS analysis, 76 patients were discharged within 2 days while 302 had extended LOS. Extended LOS was associated with higher CCI (3.86 ± 2.08 vs. 3.17 ± 1.85; p = 0.005), and home address in an at risk/distressed DCI quintile (17.9% vs. 3.95%; p = 0.018). All other demographic variables were similar for the two LOS groups. The extended length of stay group was associated with increased myelopathy indications (79.8% vs. 61.8%; p < 0.001), number of levels fused (66.2% vs. 48.7% for 4+ levels; p = 0.020), estimated blood loss (273 ± 268 vs. 197 ± 212 mL; p < 0.001), cut-to-close time (180 ± 64.7 vs. 155 ± 59.5 minutes; p < 0.001), and OR time (274 ± 72.5 vs. 235 ± 75.9 minutes; p < 0.001). On multivariate regression, diabetes (Estimate: 0.76; p = 0.046), CCI (Estimate: 0.44; p < 0.001), cut to close time (Estimate: 0.01; p = 0.021), myeloradiculopathy (Estimate: -1.12; p = 0.016), and being in the at risk/distressed DCI quintile (Estimate: 2.19; p < 0.001) were independently predictive of LOS. For readmission analysis, 42 patients experienced a readmission versus 336 who did not. The readmission group was associated with increased LOS (5.30 ± 4.40 vs. 3.87 ± 3.36 days; p = 0.011). On multivariate regression, LOS (OR: 1.12, 95% CI [1.03-1.21]; p = 0.004) and current smoking status (OR: 0.18, 95% CI [0.03-0.68]; p = 0.029) were independently predictive of readmission. Conclusion: Extended LOS after PCDF was associated with increased medical comorbidities, more distressed/at risk domestic environment, and increased complexity of surgery. 90-day readmission after PCDF was associated with increased LOS and smoking. Both increased LOS and readmission are associated with worse outcomes and increased healthcare costs. Thus, further research should focus on 1.) optimizing these risk factors that are modifiable in the perioperative period, and 2.) identifying impactful postoperative protocols to give targeted extra care to vulnerable patients with non-modifiable factors.

William Karakash

1

, Andy Ton

, Ram Alluri

, Zorica Buser

Introduction: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) is the most common surgical treatment for degenerative cervical conditions. Post-operative physical therapy (PT) has been shown to improve pain management and patient function without impacting complication rates. However, the factors associated with PT utilization following ACDF are unclear, leading to poorly understood utilization patterns. Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted using the PearlDiver Mariner database to identify patients who underwent ACDF between 2010-2022. International Classification of Disease, 9th and 10th Edition (ICD-9, ICD-10), and Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes were used to extract relevant diagnoses and procedures. Exclusion criteria included patients under 18 years of age and those with malignancy, infection, trauma, two-stage procedures, or revision within one-year post-op. PT utilization was assessed from 7 to 365 days postoperatively, with time to PT initiation calculated from the ACDF date to the first billed CPT code. Statistical analyses included student’s t-tests and chi-squared tests for continuous and categorical data, respectively. Multivariate logistic regression was employed to identify predictors of PT utilization. Results: Among 318,216 ACDF patients identified, 75,560 (23.7%) engaged in PT, while 242,656 (76.3%) did not. PT users averaged 11.12 ± 11.3 visits within the first year (median: 8 visits). PT initiation post-surgery varied: 28.3% within 6 weeks, 29.1% between 6-12 weeks, 14.0% between 12-18 weeks, and 28.5% after 18 weeks. Commercial insurance holders commenced PT earliest (102 ± 89 days), followed by Medicaid (121 ± 94 days) and Medicare (125 ± 99 days) (p < 0.001). The most used PT billing codes were therapeutic exercises (86.1% of patients), manual therapy techniques (62.6%), and neuromuscular reeducation (27.4%). Univariate analysis revealed that PT users were older (56.4 ± 11 vs 55.7 ± 11.1, p < 0.001), had higher Elixhauser Comorbidity Index scores (5.6 ± 3.9 vs 4.3 ± 3.3, p < 0.001), and had a higher family income ($79,728 vs $75,536, p < 0.001). Multivariate analysis identified several factors associated with increased PT utilization: commercial insurance (OR 4.36), preoperative opioid usage (OR 1.37), cervical radiculopathy (OR 1.37), cervical myelopathy (OR 1.31), depression (OR 1.21), obesity (1.13), female sex (OR 1.09), and multi-level procedure (1.04). The likelihood of PT utilization increased with the number of cervical levels fused from two levels (OR 1.05) to five levels (OR 1.36). Conclusion: This analysis reveals significant variability in the timing and utilization of physical therapy following ACDF, with only a quarter of patients engaging in post-operative PT. Factors such as commercial insurance, pre-existing conditions, and surgical complexity increase PT usage. The variability in PT timing and utilization highlights the need for developing standardized post-operative care protocols. Future research should focus on determining optimal PT timing and duration to improve patient outcomes following ACDF, potentially leading to more effective post-operative rehabilitation strategies.

## P184: Incidence of adjacent segment degeneration after multi-level posterior cervical instrumented fusion to C7

Torsten Fras

1

, Sebastian Fras

2

1
Institute for Spinal Surgery, Department of Spine Surgery, Broomall, United States, 
2
Thomas Jefferson Sidney Kimmel Medical College, Philadelphia, United States
Introduction: Adjacent segment degeneration (ASD) after spinal fusion is postulated to be related to increased biomechanical stress exerted on unfused spinal levels adjacent to a fusion. In the cervical spine, the C7-T1 level is a junctional level, between the mobile cervical segments and the relatively immobile thoracic vertebrae. Some surgeons are concerned that cervical fusions ending at C7 are at significant risk for C7-T1 degeneration; in such circumstances, it is suggested that the unfused C7-T1 level acts as an area of concentrated increased biomechanical stress (a “hinge”) between the fixed thoracic and cervical segments with a high likelihood of future degeneration. Therefore, in the setting of a posterior cervical instrumented fusion (PCIF) that ends at C7, many surgeons recommend extending the fusion to T1. However, such an extension of the fusion carries associated potential morbidity. Furthermore, it has not been clearly established that PCIF to the C7 level definitively increases the risk of C7-T1 degeneration. This study seeks to evaluate the incidence of clinically significant C7-T1 degeneration in the setting of long (4+ segments) PCIF ending at the C7 level. Material and Methods: A retrospective chart review investigated all patients in a single practice undergoing PCIF of 4 or more segments, with C7 as the terminal caudal level, between 2012-2022. All patients were followed clinically and radiographically for a minimum of 2 years. At final follow up, patients were assessed for C7-T1 degeneration based on any of the following inclusion criteria: surgery having been performed or recommended extending the instrumented fusion to T1 or distally; or radiographic findings of C7-T1 degeneration with clinical correlation (neck and/or radicular symptoms, new myelopathic findings). The incidence of C7-T1 degeneration in the subject population was then determined. Results: 32 patients underwent minimum 4 segment PCIF between 2012 and 2022. All had minimum 2-year clinical and radiographic follow up; mean follow-up was 82 months. All cases used the same instrumentation (Globus Quartex), and all used local bone graft with Grafton demineralized bone matrix for bone grafting. Thirteen patients underwent C4-7 PCIF; 18 underwent C3-7 PCIF; 1 underwent C2-7 PCIF. There were no cases of hardware failure / malposition, pseudarthrosis, vascular injury, dural tear, or deep infection. Two patients experienced transient C5 nerve root palsy, both recovering completely; there were no other cases of neurologic deficit. One patient underwent further surgical treatment of C7-T1 degeneration with fusion to T1. There were no other cases of clinical or radiographic C7-T1 degeneration. There were no cases of ASD proximal to the fusion. Conclusion: Some reports suggest ASD after anterior cervical fusion is approximately 3% per year. In this study, long PCIF constructs in which 4 or more vertebrae were fused to C7 were found to have a 3.1% incidence of ASD after a mean follow up of nearly 7 years. This is lower than predicted from previous studies, and suggests that in fusions to C7, the C7-T1 level need not automatically be included in a PCIF if there is no other compelling pathology at this level.

## P185: Isolated decompression for bilateral C1-C2 acessory facet joint with compressive myelopathy: case report and narrative review

Erenaldo de Souza Rodrigues Júnior

, Carlos Alberto Assunção Filho

Introduction: Upper cervical spinal stenosis associated with the C1-C2 accessory facet is a very rare entity. Salunke et. al. in 2013 reported for the first time a case of bilateral C1-C2 accessory facet joint. Since then, only a few cases have been described. In 2019, Chowdhury, Forhad H. et al. documented a case of bilateral C1-C2 accessory facet joint treated with decompression and arthrodesis, due to compressive myelopathy and preoperative instability. We present here a rare case of upper cervical stenosis with myelopathy caused by the C1-C2 accessory facet joint, without signs of instability.
