## P613: Interpretation of high cervical injuries by doctors, students and specialists: where we are?

Mateus Leal

1

, Ramon Guerra Barbosa

2

, Felipe Fernandes Leão

1

, Luís Fernando Weber De Oliveira

1

, Yan Silva

1

, Eduardo Gil França Gomes

1

, Cleston Paiva

1

1
Hospital Geral do Estado da Bahia, Salvador, Brazil,

2

Chicoutimi, Quebec, Canada

Introduction: Spinal cord trauma is a recognized public health problem. It occurs in 2-6% of emergency traumas but is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Incorrect radiographic diagnoses account for up to 20% of undiagnosed injuries. The study aims to assess the interpretation of LCA images by orthopedic doctors, medical students, general practitioners, and specialists. Material and Methods: This work is an exploratory, observational, cross-sectional study through an electronic questionnaire distributed via digital media and answered by medical students, general practitioners, residents, and specialists. It was divided into a demographic session, another with images of various injuries for analysis between normal and pathological, a multiple-choice section on diagnoses, and an evaluation of knowledge of classic imaging parameters. Results: Out of 49 responses, 32% were residents, 45% specialists, 10% general practitioners, and 8% students. Only 26% reported having participated in any prior cervical radiology training, and 51% had witnessed a situation where the correct diagnosis was not made during the initial care. In the normal vs. pathological session, a traumatic C2-C3 spondylolisthesis was identified in 98%, while a CT scan of C1-C2 rotatory instability (IRAA) in pediatrics was identified by only 38%. A normal coronal CT scan was identified by 73%. In the multiple-choice section, an axial MRI slice showing a transverse ligament injury (LLT) was identified by 22%, with 28% mistaking it for a C2 lateral mass fracture. Occipito-cervical dissociation (DOC) was identified by 39% in another image. In the final section, Harris' rule (HR) was identified by 43%, Powers’ ratio (PR) by 69%, and Wackenheim line (WL) by 53%. Regarding normality measures, anterior C1-C2 interval (ADI) was the most recognized at 63%, while the 12mm value for HR was identified by 36%, with 47% attributing this value to PR and 16% to the A-O Interval. Conclusion: LCAs are an important factor in morbidity and mortality. Although most are stable injuries, accurate identification is critical. Our data showed significant difficulty in identifying DOC and IRAA. More evident injuries had higher accuracy rates, supporting the reliability of responses. The most recognized measure was ADI, but pathological images were not identified, raising questions about the lack of systematic radiographic evaluation. The study points to a significant gap in the training of doctors and specialists, and further research is needed to better understand the reproducibility of the results.

## P615: Multiple vertebral fractures with surgical indication in a pediatric patient

Diego Alvarez

1

, Francoise Descazeaux

1

, Maria José Tauton

1

, Carlos Huaiquilaf

1

1

Hospital Dr Exequiel Gonzales Cortes, Servicio de Traumatología, Unidad de Columna, Santiago, Chile

Introduction: Vertebral fractures in pediatric patients are relatively uncommon, representing approximately 2-5% of all pediatric fractures. The nature and location of these fractures vary with age: cervical fractures are more frequent in children under five, while thoracolumbar fractures are more common in those over ten. This review discusses the mechanisms, classifications, management strategies, and outcomes associated with multiple cervical and thoracolumbar fractures in children, illustrated by a case study of a 12-year-old girl. Materials and Methods: A comprehensive literature review was conducted, focusing on the incidence, causes, and treatment of vertebral fractures in the pediatric population. Sources included peer-reviewed articles, clinical guidelines, and case reports. A specific case was examined: a 12-year-old female with obesity who sustained multiple vertebral fractures from a high-energy motor vehicle accident (MVA). Clinical assessments included radiographic imaging and neurological evaluations. Results: Pediatric vertebral fractures account for about 1% of all pediatric fractures, with no significant gender association noted. The leading causes include motor vehicle accidents (58%), falls from height, sports injuries, and child abuse. Although many cases do not present with neurological deficits, potential long-term complications such as increased kyphosis and accelerated disc degeneration can occur. The most common classification systems utilized are the TLICS and AO systems, although these have been primarily validated in adult populations. In the case study, the patient presented with several significant injuries: an AO B2 fracture at C6-C7, an AO A0 fracture at T5, and a B2 fracture at T6-T7, all without neurological compromise. Given the instability of the fractures, surgical intervention was warranted. The management involved an anterior cervical discectomy and fusion at C6-C7, alongside posterior instrumented arthrodesis from T5 to T9. Conclusions: Pediatric vertebral fractures, while rare, can lead to serious complications if not properly managed. The presented case underscores the importance of timely surgical intervention in cases of unstable fractures to prevent long-term sequelae. The patient demonstrated a favorable outcome, returning to normal activities without neurological deficits six months post-accident. This case emphasizes the need for a thorough understanding of the unique characteristics of pediatric vertebral fractures and the importance of using validated classification systems for appropriate management. Further studies are necessary to clarify the incidence of multiple vertebral fractures in children and to refine treatment protocols tailored to this vulnerable population.

## P617: Case of instable Anderson D’Alonso type III fracture combined with Hangman’s fracture treated by navigated CT assisted percutaneous Magerl ang Judet technique

Peter Hudak

, Kristian Varga

, Martin Srdliak

, Milan Liska

, Benedikt Trnovec

1

Bory Hospital, Neurosurgery, Bratislava

Odontoid C2 fracture is more common fracture in elderly population, less frequently in younger patients. 50% of odontoid fractures of all cervical fractures are patients over 80 years of age. Low-energy trauma in elderly population is typical for incidence of this fracture type. In comparison young patients are linked to high energy trauma as a result of fall from heights or motor vehicle accidents. The mechanism of injury is mainly hyperflection with the anterior displacement of odontoid. Hyperextension displaces the odontoid posteriorly. Classification for odontoid fractures commonly used is Anderson D’Alonzo classification which has three types. Type I demonstrates the avulsion af the odontoid tip. This type rarely causes neurologic deficit and is treated by conservative way. Type II fractures are the most common. The fracture is presented in the waist of the odontoid near to the body of the C2. It could be expalined that the trabecular structure of the bone is thinner in comparison with other parts of odontoid body. This type is characterised by increased communication between fragments and leads to greather instability. Type III extends from the proximal anterior aspect to the C2 body. The Harms technique is now considered as the gold standard to stabilize C1-C2 cervical spine. It has been reported to decrease the risk of vertebral artery injury. However, the risk of vascular injury does not totally disappear, particularly due to the proximity of the trans-isthmic C2 screw with the foramen transversarium of C2. Hangman fracture is divided into four types based on the most widely accepted Levine-Edward classification. Many scholars advocate early surgical treatment. C2 transpedicular screw fixation proposed by Judet in 1964 is called physiological reconstruction because of its low trauma, immediate stability and maximum retention of the physiological functions of adjacent segments. Indication of the fusion in the impaired segment gives us several ways. The main goal of the modern spine surgery is the miniinvasivity which is also applicable in posterior approaches of the upper cervical spine. Navigation and the peroperative CT or mobile CT allows us to perform less invasive spine surgery also in cervical spine surgery Judet and also Harms technique can be performed by percutaneous way . The accuracy of spine navigation increases the security of selected procedure.

## P618: Surgical management of subaxial cervical injuries: is a combined approachs necessary?

Ignacio Cirillo

1

, Harold Sherman Fuentes

1

, Juan José Zamorano

1

, Carlos Tapia

2

, Marcos Gimbernat

1

, Ignacio Farías

1

, Daniela Novoa

3

1
Hospital del Trabajador, Equipo de Columna, Santiago, Chile,

2
Hospital del Trabajador, Equipo de Columna, Fellow AO, Santiago, Chile,

3

Universidad de los Andes, Residente Orthopedic, Santiago, Chile

Introduction: Subaxial cervical fractures present a clinical challenge due to their complexity and associated neurological risks. The choice of surgical approach depends on the nature and severity of the injury. The purpose of this study was to analyze anterior, posterior, and combined approaches performed in these fractures, highlighting their characteristics and associations. Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 43 patients with surgically treated subaxial cervical fractures between 2015 and 2020 in a specialized center. Data were extracted from clinical records and image analysis through the institutional system. Demographic data, fracture type, surgical approach, complications, and hospital stay were collected. Results: 86% of patients were male, with a mean age of 44 years. The most frequent fracture was type C AOSpine (55%), followed by B2 (16%), with the C6C7 segment most affected (27%). Anterior approaches were performed in 76% of cases, while 18.6% underwent a combined approach. Of the combined group, 62.5% had delayed surgeries with an average interval of 6 days between procedures. The hospital stay in the combined group averaged 69 days, significantly longer than in the anterior group (P: 0.018), and the most common levels for the combined approach were C4C5 and C5C6, with no significant differences compared to other groups. The combined approach was more associated with the N4 modifier in AOSpine classification (37.5% vs. 9.1%) and a higher proportion of postoperative complications (62%) compared to the anterior group (27%), without statistical significance. Conclusion: The most frequently used approach was anterior, followed by combined and posterior. Combined approaches, though necessary in more complex cases, were associated with a higher proportion of complications and prolonged hospital stays. These results highlight the importance of carefully selecting the most appropriate approach based on the severity of the fracture to improve outcomes and reduce complications.

## P619: Goel-Harms C1-C2 osteosynthesis: a “bloodless technique” in microsurgical dissection of the perivertebral venous plexus and C2 ganglion with a technical variation

Giuseppe Barbagallo

1

, Giacomo Cammarata

1

, Erica Grasso

1

, Giulio Bonomo

1

, Francesco Certo

1

1

University Hospital “G. Rodolico - San Marco”, Neurosurgery, Catania, Italy

Introduction: The C1-C2 osteosynthesis technique according to Goel-Harms has been described and reported as one of the most effective and biomechanically robust techniques. This method and its variants have been utilized for different traumatic and non-traumatic conditions. While this surgical approach can ensure a very solid fusion, it presents technically complex steps, particularly concerning the dissection of the perivertebral venous plexus and the identification of the screw entry point in C1. Several authors suggest resection of the C2 ganglion in this context. Although the utility of this maneuver is clear, its safety in terms of outcome is debatable. In this study, we propose a “bloodless” microsurgical technique involving coagulation and dissection of the perivertebral venous plexus and the C2 ganglion. This allows subperiosteal exposure of the entry point of the C1 lateral mass without sectioning the ganglion, but rather gently retracting it during instrument insertion maneuvers. Material and Methods: The proposed technique was applied to 27 patients who underwent C1-C2 osteosynthesis using the Goel-Harms technique. All vertebral fractures were classified according to the AOSpine classification and the Anderson-D'Alonzo classification. All patients underwent pre- and post-operative supine cervical X-rays (AP and lateral), MRI, and CT scans. The effectiveness and safety of the proposed technique were evaluated in terms of short-term clinical outcome (Frankel Grading Classification), quantification of blood loss, and hospitalization length. Descriptive statistical analysis and Pearson correlation tests were performed using RStudio software version 23.12.0. Results: The analysis included 27 patients with a mean age of 58 years. Nine patients presented with an odontoid fracture, with 4 type II fractures and 5 type III fractures according to the Anderson-D'Alonzo classification. In 3 patients, atlantoaxial instability was associated with the presence of a retro-odontoid cystic pannus, and in 1 patient with os odontoideum. The remaining cases (14/27) involved a post-traumatic fracture of C1-C2 associated with dislocation/translation. The mean pre-operative hemoglobin level was 13.82 g/dl, while the post-operative level was 11.7 g/dl, resulting in a mean loss of 2.1 g/dl of hemoglobin (R = 0.886; p < 0.01). The mean pre-operative hematocrit was 41.63%, and the post-operative value was 35.59% (R = 0.875; p < 0.01). The mean post-operative hospital stay was 6 days ± 6.1. No patient exhibited a worsening of neurological status. Five of the six patients with neurological impairment at admission showed improvement in pre-operative motor-sensory deficits. In all cases, post-operative CT scans and/or cervical spine X-rays demonstrated correct positioning of the instrumentation without complications. Only one case exhibited transient unilateral occipital neuralgia (Arnold's neuralgia) post-operatively. Conclusion: Accurate subperiosteal dissection of the C1-C2 joint, accurate dissection of the venous plexus and preservation of the C2 ganglion allow for effective bleeding control and safe preservation of the relevant vascular and neural structures. Gentle, intermittent upward and downward retraction of the C2 ganglion after dissection is feasible and does not compromise anatomical exposure. We believe this technique, by significantly reducing intraoperative bleeding, can enhance surgeon's confidence in identifying anatomical landmarks during C1-C2 surgery, reducing potential post-operative neurological disturbances resulting from sectioning of C2 ganglion.

## P620: Immediate supraphysiologic load-bearing of the spine appears safe after gunshot-related spinal cord injury: a case-control study

Hirofumi Kusumoto

1

, Isabel Alvarez

1

, Dudley Fukunaga

2

, Sean Dreyer

2

, Kevin Rolfe

1

1
Harbor UCLA Medical Center, Orthopaedic Surgery, Torrance, United States,

2

Rancho Los Amigos National Rehabilitation Center, Orthopaedic Surgery, Downey, United States

Introduction: Gun violence is a leading cause of spinal cord injury in the US civilian population. This mechanism usually results in a stable injury pattern to the spine, however there is little existing literature regarding the safety of early supraphysiologic loadbearing of the spine from a structural and neurologic standpoint. Material and Methods: A retrospective chart review of eighty-five patients from a national spinal cord injury rehabilitation center was conducted. Patients were allocated to two groups: those who initiated resistance training exercises (e.g. free weight or weight machine exercises, resistance band exercises, or ergometer use on a resistance setting) within three weeks of date of injury and those who began after three weeks. Primary endpoints included change in American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) grade and need for spinal surgery for any reason following resistance training exercises completed during the acute inpatient rehabilitation stay. Results: Mean follow up interval was 59.7 ± 7.4 weeks for the entire study population. No patients sustained a neurologic decline or required secondary surgery for late deformity correction or any other reason regardless of time to resistance training initiation. There was no difference in ASIA grade improvement rates across either group. Conclusion: Immediate resistance training as part of a rehabilitation regimen for gunshot spinal cord injury appears safe.

## P622: Neurological manifestation in thoracolumbar junction traumatic injuries

Oleksii Nekhlopochyn

1

, Vadim Verbov

2

, Ievgen Cheshuk

2

, Milan Vorodi

2

1
Romodanov Neurosurgery Institute, Spine Neurosurgery, Kyiv, Ukraine,

2

Romodanov Neurosurgery Institute, Restorative Neurosurgery Department, Kyiv, Ukraine

Introduction: Traumatic injuries to the thoracolumbar junction account for over 60% of all injuries to the thoracolumbar spine. The neurological symptomatology accompanying injuries at this level is characterized by diverse patterns of both motor and sensory dysfunction, which are determined by the topographic-anatomical features of this area. Neurological deficits may be caused by conductive, segmental, and radicular disturbances. The aim of the study is to determine the nature and frequency of neurological disorders in patients with spine and spinal cord trauma at the level of the thoracolumbar junction, depending on the likely substrate of the traumatic impact. Materials and Methods: An analysis of the neurological status assessment results of 101 patients who suffered spine and spinal cord trauma at the level of the thoracolumbar junction was conducted. The average age of the patients was 41 years (95% confidence interval - 36-44). The majority of the patients were male (75.25%). The number of motor segments with signs of upper and lower motor neuron damage, and dermatomes with sensory function impairment of radicular, segmental, or conductive types were determined. Results: The analysis revealed that 83.5% of motor segments with dysfunction exhibited clinical signs consistent with lower motor neuron damage. In cases of spinal cord injury at the Th11 level with ASIA A functional class, lower motor neuron dysfunction was observed in 73.33% of cases. For ASIA B and ASIA C, these figures were 65% and 25%, respectively, while in ASIA D, all patients displayed only upper motor neuron insufficiency. At the Th12 level, upper motor neuron damage was responsible for clinical symptoms in 42.86% of ASIA C cases and in 66.67% of ASIA D cases. For spinal cord injuries at the L1 level, upper motor neuron damage was noted only in patients classified as ASIA D (42.86%), while more severe functional impairments were predominantly associated with peripheral-type disturbances. All injuries at the L2 level were characterized by varying degrees of lower motor neuron damage, which influenced the ASIA functional classification. In the assessment of sensory impairments, 41.3% of dermatomes with sensory disturbances were found to have clinical signs indicative of traumatic root damage, 57.9% exhibited segmental-type impairments, and 28.9% demonstrated conduction-type disturbances. Conclusion: The data obtained indicate a significant role of segmental disturbances in forming the symptom complex in patients with spine and spinal cord trauma at the level of the thoracolumbar junction.

## P623: Successful nonoperative treatment of select AO-B3 thoracolumbar injury patterns

Ethan Sheppard

1

, Saurabh Rawall

1

, Gerald McGwin

2

, Luke Hiatt

1

1
University of Alabama at Birmingham Heersink School of Medicine, Orthopaedic Surgery, Birmingham, United States,

2

University of Alabama at Birmingham Heersink School of Medicine, Epidemiology, Birmingham, United States

Introduction: The AO Spine fracture classification system has been well-validated as a fracture morphology classification system. However, the optimal treatment for some of the fracture patterns has not been fully elucidated. B3 injuries are defined as extension-type injuries that result in failure of the anterior column due to tension injury to the disc and/or vertebral body. B3 injuries often occur in ankylotic disorders, including ankylosing spondylitis (AS) and diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH). This can result in additional disruption of the middle and posterior columns, resulting in an unstable injury pattern. Presence of neurological deficit or involvement of the posterior column warrants surgery. However, optimal treatment of B3 injuries with normal neurology and intact posterior column has not been rigorously studied. We propose that B3 injuries with intact posterior tension band may be amenable to non-operative care. This study sought to evaluate the outcomes of non-operative treatment of B3 injuries with intact posterior tension bands. Objective: To identify AO-B3 injury patterns amenable to non-operative management. Material and Methods: We retrospectively evaluated thoracic vertebral fractures treated by the orthopaedic surgery department at our institution from January 1, 2015, to December 15, 2023. Out of 2,086 identified cases, 57 patients with AO-B3 fractures were selected based on strict inclusion criteria, and 38 had a minimum follow-up period of 3 months. No patients with spinal cord injuries were included in the study. Of these 38 patients, 32 underwent operative treatment and 6 underwent nonoperative treatment. Amongst those patients that underwent operative treatment, 19 patients had multiple spinal fractures, 6 patients had AS, and 13 patients had DISH. For the remaining 6 patients who were managed non surgically we recorded the demographic data, radiographic measurements, and clinical outcomes were extracted from electronic medical records. Due to the small number of patients in the cohorts, statistical analysis for differences in outcomes was not performed. Results: Of the patients that underwent nonoperative treatment, 2 had multiple spinal fractures, none had a diagnosis of AS, and 4 had a diagnosis of DISH. None of these patients had any of the tracked medical complications including DVT, UTI or pneumonia. Average hospital LOS was 8 days, 16.67% of patients were admitted to ICU, and none of the patients were rehospitalized or converted to surgery. Conclusion: Surgical management is often selected for patients with AO-B3 thoracic injuries due to concerns about instability, particularly in cases with spinal cord injury, ankylosing spondylitis (AS), or posterior tension band disruption. However, our study suggests that non-operative management can be effectively employed in AO-B3 injuries without these complicating factors. Additionally, our findings indicate that patients with diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) can also be successfully managed non-operatively. This approach not only reduces medical complications, hospital stays, and healthcare costs but also eliminates the inherent risks associated with surgery. To validate these observations, a larger multi-center study is warranted.

## P624: Return to work rate and identification of influential factors after traumatic thoracolumbar fractures without spinal cord injury: a systematic review

Mathijs Suijkerbuijk

1

, Ameijden, Van Sara

2,3

, Cranenbroek Daan

1

, Egmond, Van Pim

1

, Joosen Margot

4

, Jongh Mariska

3 4

, Ruth Geuze

1

1
Elizabeth Tweesteden Hospital, Orthopedic Surgery, Tilburg, Netherlands,

2
Elisabeth Tweesteden Hospital, General Surgery, Tilburg, Netherlands,

3
Network Emergency Care Brabant, Tilburg, Netherlands,

4

Tilburg University, Tranzo Scientific Center for Care and Well-Being, Tilburg, Netherlands

Introduction: Traumatic fractures of the thoracolumbar spine without spinal cord injury (SCI) are considered a major public health issue due to the increasing incidence, a negative impact on the quality of life and the significant socio-economic consequences. The current literature is unclear about the return to work (RTW) rate after traumatic thoracolumbar fractures without SCI and which predictive factors affect the ability to RTW. This scoping review aims to determine the RTW rate and identify influential factors for RTW following traumatic thoracolumbar fractures without SCI. Materials and Methods: A search was performed in the Embase, Medline (OvidSP), Web of Science, Cochrane, PubMed, and Google Scholar databases up to January 2024. A study was eligible if it met the following inclusion criteria: (1) traumatic thoracolumbar fractures, (2) no SCI, (3) reporting RTW (4) study design was a prospective cohort, retrospective cohort or case-control study. RTW was defined as a return to previous employment, being either heavy or sedentary labor. Studies were excluded if the article was not written in English and no full text was available. The risk of bias was assessed in all eligible studies using the Quality in Prognostic Studies (QUIPS) tool. Results: A total of 23 publications met our inclusion criteria and demonstrated a moderate to high risk of bias. The overall mean RTW rate was 75% (median [IQR], 0.74 [0.29]), with an average follow-up of 38.9 months. When stratified by treatment type, the mean RTW rate was 79% (median [IQR], 0.79 [0.24]) following non-operative treatment, with a mean follow-up of 32.7 months, compared to 66% (median [IQR], 0.67 [0.41]) after operative treatment, with a mean follow-up of 52.7 months. Included studies identified the following influencing factors: younger age and fewer comorbidities were associated with a higher likelihood of RTW. Additionally, the absence of financial support or occupational healthcare negatively impacted RTW rates. Conclusion: This review demonstrates that 25% of the patients with traumatic thoracolumbar fractures without SCI was unable to RTW after an average follow-up of 38.9 months. The findings suggest that patients managed non-operatively have a higher RTW rate compared to those who underwent surgical intervention. Key factors associated with a higher RTW rate include younger age, absence of comorbidities, well-structured occupational healthcare, and lack of comprehensive insurance policies. However, these conclusions should be interpreted with caution due to the moderate to high risk of bias in the included studies. To enhance patient-centered care following traumatic thoracolumbar fractures, it is pivotal to determine predictive factors to improve RTW after thoracolumbar fractures and to provide appropriate support to enhance RTW.

## P625: Risk factor and mortality prevention: an analysis of hospital mortality in thoracolumbar spinal cord injuries in 525 cases in Germany

Jonas Krueckel

1

, Melanie Schindler

1

, Volker Alt

1

, Siegmund Lang

1

1

University Hospital Regensburg, Department of Trauma Surgery, Regensburg, Germany

Introduction: This study aims to analyze the relationships between comorbidities, injury location, and demographic characteristics and their influence on hospital mortality in adult patients with thoracolumbar spinal cord injuries. Given the severe consequences of these injuries, it is essential to identify possible risk factors for hospital mortality. Material and Methods: This study utilized data from the InEK GmbH database for the year 2022, which contains comprehensive information on Diagnosis-Related Groups (DRGs) and hospital billing in Germany. We included patients aged 18 years and older with thoracolumbar spinal cord injuries. The hospital mortality rate was determined, and differences in comorbidities and accompanying diseases were analyzed using the Chi-square test. Odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) were calculated to identify potential risk factors for hospital mortality. Results: The study included 525 patients with a hospital mortality rate of 5.7%. Thoracic spinal cord injuries were more common at 73.9% (n = 388) than lumbar (26.1%, n = 137), but did not show a significantly increased risk of death (OR = 1.44, CI:0.57-3.6, p = 0.44). In the older patient group (> 80 years), both incidence (10.97 per million per year) and mortality risk (OR = 4.65, CI: 2.09-10.24, p = 0.0002) were higher compared to younger patients (7.2 per million per year for 18-80-year-olds). Significantly associated with increased hospital mortality were acute hemorrhagic anemia (OR = 4.33, 95% CI: 2.04-9.18, p < 0.001) and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (OR = 12.45, 95% CI: 5.28-19.23, p < 0.001). Non-uncontrolled Type II diabetes mellitus (OR = 2.34, 95% CI: 0.88-6.45, p = 0.10), essential hypertension without hypertensive crisis (OR = 1.36, 95% CI: 0.61-3.07, p = 0.44), and the pre-existing use of anticoagulants (OR = 1.67, 95% CI: 0.61-4.54, p = 0.31) were identified as potential, but statistically non-significant, risk factors. Conclusion: Especially older patients and patients with certain pre-existing conditions show an increased risk of hospital mortality after a thoracolumbar spinal cord injury. Therefore, the prevention of complications and adequate treatment of existing diseases are critical to mitigate the severe impacts of spinal cord injuries.

## P628: Treatment of post traumatic thoracolumbar fractures. SpineJack vs short arthrodesis vs bracing: a randomized controlled trial

Introduction: In the traumatic A1 to A3 vertebral fractures surgery is increasingly preferred to conservative treatment to avoid inactivity and diminution of quality of life (QoL). Therefore, we designed and conducted the first randomized controlled trial to compare clinical and radiological outcomes of these fractures treated with posterior short arthrodesis, SJ or bracing. Our aim is to enroll 300 patients, 100 for every treatment type, over 18 months. We present the preliminary (12 months) results here. Material and Methods: We enrolled every patient between 18 and 65 y/o with one to two traumatic fracture types A1, A2, A3, from T10 to L4, without neurological deficits between 09.2022 and 03.2024. Patients with A1 fractures were randomized between bracing or SJ and A2, and A3 were randomized between SJ and short arthrodesis. Subjects were followed at admission, discharge, 6 and 12 months, either clinically (VAS, ODI, and EQ-5D-5L) or radiologically (local and vertebral kyphosis, disc ratios, vertebral height). Results: After 12 months, in our preliminary analysis, we found no significant differences in postoperative pain in the SJ vs. short arthrodesis arm, while operative time and discharge time were shorter for SJ. The increase in vertebral body height and volume was approximately > 25% after SJ. SJ patients had non-inferior VK e LK angles correction. In SJ vs. bracing arm, we found significant pain reduction, lower rates of kyphosis progression, better QoL in SJ patients, and an improvement in disc ratio parameters. No significant adverse events in SJ positioning were observed. Conclusion: Our preliminary results showed satisfactory outcomes in neurologically intact thoracolumbar A1 to A3 fractures. SJ leads to shorter operative and discharge time, good VB angles, and restoration of diameters compared to short arthrodesis. SJ proved in pain relief, improved quality of life, and reduced risk of kyphosis compared to bracing.

## P629: Do all spinal injuries need decompression?

Shah Alam

1

, Abdullah Al Mamun

2

, Ziaul Hasan

2

1
Bangladesh Spine and Orthopedic Hospital, BSOH, Spine and Orthopedic Surgery, Dhaka, Bangladesh,

2

National Institute of Traumatology and Orthopedic Rehabilitation, NITOR, Spine and Orthopedic Surgery, Dhaka, Bangladesh

Background: Spinal Injury is a very common and devastating injury in developing country as well as developed world. Mostly surgery is the management of choice. But its been a long debate whether only stabilization is enough or decompression is also necessary while treating spinal injuries. The purpose of this study is to investigate the clinical outcome of posterior stabilization without decompression for thoracolumbar burst fractures. Materials and Method: 48 consecutive cases of thoracolumbar fractures involving T11-L2 stabilized by a pedicle screw system were reviewed. Neither reduction of the height of a fractured body nor any decompression procedure was added during surgery. 40 patients had incomplete paraplegia; 8 patient had complete paraplegia. Neurological recovery and remodeling of the spinal canal were evaluated. Neurological status was evaluated at the time of injury, just before and after surgery, and at final follow-up. The degree of spinal canal compromise was assessed using axial CT scan images. The duration of follow-up averaged 12 weeks. no significant correlation was observed between the degree of canal compromise and the severity of the neurological deficit. Result: Canal compromise had decreased significantly 3-4 weeks after injury. 25 patients regained neurology at the final follow-up. The mean pre-operative kyphotic deformity was 22.75 ± 4.690 which became 10.53 ± 3.11°at final follow up. ODI improved from a pre-operative score of 67.20 to a final 25.08. Conclusion: This study suggests that the effect of decompressing thoracolumbar fractures with neurological deficits remains unclear and questions the need to operate simply to remove retropulsed bone fragments. Harborview Medical Center, Department of Orthopaedics and Sports Medicine, University of Washington, Seattle, United States,

Ganga Hospital, Department of Orthopaedics and Spine Surgery, Coimbatore, India,

Prince Mohammed Bin Abdulaziz Hospital, Department of Neurosurgery, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia,

Klinika Úrazovej Chirurgie , .D.Roosevelta, Banská Bystrica, Slovakia,

21
AO Foundation, Stettbachstrasse 6, 8600 Dübendorf, Switzerland,

22
Combined Neurosurgical and Orthopedic Spine Program, Vancouver General Hospital, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada,

23

University Medical Centers, Utrecht, Netherlands

Objective: To compare the functional outcomes following non-operative and operative management of incomplete (A3) and complete (A4) thoracolumbar burst fractures. Methods: A prospective observational international multi-centre cohort study (AO Spine TLA3-A4) was conducted examining the management of thoracolumbar fractures. After stratification using the AO Spine Thoracolumbar Injury Classification System, the outcomes following either non-operative or operative management of these fractures was analyzed. Outcomes of interest were ODI at discharge, the absolute and relative improvement in Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) between discharge and 12 months follow-up. A multivariable mixed model for repeated measurement was used assess ODI at discharge differences. Kaplan-Meier curves were generated and compared by the log-rank test. Multivariable Cox regression models were constructed. Both, the mixed model and the Cox regression models were adjusted using the key covariates of age, sex, an interaction between fracture type and treatment type (open short or long posterior fixation, anterior alone or combined anterior/posterior fixation and percutaneous posterior fixation) and working status and additionally ODI at discharge for relative ODI improvement. Results: 198 thoracolumbar burst fractures were identified with incomplete (A3) burst fractures (58.6%) being more common than the complete (A4) burst injuries (41.4%). The rate of operative management was similar for A4 fractures compared to A3 fractures (50.8% versus 49.2%) but the rate of nonoperative management was significantly higher among A3 than among A4 fractures (73.7% vs 26.3%), p = 0.001). A multivariable mixed model for repeated measurement did not show significant differences for ODI at baseline between the treatment groups for A3 fractures (p = 0.227) or A4 fractures (p = 0.096). Kaplan Meier curves did not show significant difference in relative and absolute median time improvement. Multivariable Cox regression model demonstrated no significant treatment difference in achieving in ODI improvement of more than 12.8 points from baseline within one year after treatment in either the A3 fracture (OR 0.67, 95% CI 0.42-1.06, p = 0.090) or A4 fracture subgroups (OR 0.75,95% CI 0.42-1.34, p = 0.329). Achieving an absolute ODI improvement of 20 or less as an outcome within the two patient groups was also similar for A3 fractures (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.48-1.16, p = 0.190) and A4 fractures (OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.38-1.33, p = 0.287). However, when comparing surgical subgroups with nonsurgical treatment, open short or long segment posterior fusion within patients with an A3 fracture however indicated a higher chance for absolute ODI improvement compared to nonsurgical treatment (OR 1.68, 95% CI 1.03-2.74, p = 0.04). There was no significant difference in achieving ODI improvement for different surgical subgroups compared to non-surgically treated patients. Conclusions: In general, no differences were found in relative and absolute ODI improvement, regardless of whether operative or non-operative management was instituted for both the A3 and A4 fracture morphologies. Exception was the higher chance of absolute ODI improvement through the application of open short or long segment posterior fusion compared to nonsurgical treatment within patients with A3 fractures. Further larger studies are required to assess the utility of different surgical techniques A3 and A4 fracture morphologies.

## P631: Functional outcome of short segment pedicle screw insertion in thoracolumbar vertebrae burst fractures

Introduction: The goal of operative treatment of thoracolumbar spinal fractures is to protect neurological function and to restore spinal stability and alignment. The surgical strategy chosen should correct segmental kyphotic deformity and prevent late instability and pain while permitting early ambulation and return to function. Short-segment instrumentation limits the number of segments instrumented to the very minimum necessary to restore sagittal balance and stabilize the fracture. Material and Methods: The study was conducted at the Department of Orthopaedics, Government Medical College, Kota, Rajasthan, India. 30 Patients with thoracolumbar vertebral burst fractures were taken up for the study. No patient had any other complication such as implant failure, infection, neurological deterioration etc. Conclusion: Short Segment Pedicle Screw Instrumentation in thoracolumbar vertebral burst fractures is a viable treatment option that compared to long segment fixation provides better mobility, less blood los and lower operative times and gives excellent results with respect to union and pain outcomes.

## P632: Challenging decision-making in spinal firearm and stab injuries - Case series from a Brazilian trauma center

Yan Silva

1,2

, Luís Fernando Weber De Oliveira

1,2

, Felipe Fernandes Leão

1,2

, Ramon Guerra Barbosa

3

, Rony Brito Fernandes

2

, Eduardo Gil França Gomes

2

1
Hospital Ortopédico do Estado, Spine Surgery, Salvador,

2
Hospital Geral do Estado, Trauma RaquiMedular - TRM, Trauma RaquiMedular - TRM, Salvador,

3

Hopital de Chicoutimi, Neurosurgery, Chicoutimi, Canada

Introduction: Urban violence in developing countries is a significant problem that results in daily victims. Firearm and stab injuries pose a formidable challenge for spine surgeons. The aim of this study was to discuss complex therapeutic decisions in extreme cases of firearm and stab injuries managed at a trauma center in Brazil. Materials and Methods: Case 01: A 20-year-old male with a gunshot wound to the mouth was intubated and immobilized. General surgery evaluation suspected esophageal injury, but neurological function remained intact. CT imaging revealed a projectile fragment in the anterior space between the atlas and the basium. Expectant management was chosen, and the patient had a favorable outcome. Case 02: A 30-year-old male presented with a stab wound to the posterior neck, without neurological deficits. Cervical angiography indicated a knife fragment located approximately 1 mm from the V3/V4 segment of the right vertebral artery. Surgical intervention was performed, resulting in a successful removal of the foreign body. Case 03: A 30 y-o male sustained a gunshot wound to the spine, leading to partial deficit, at the level of L1. The entry wound was in the thoracolumbar region, and imaging revealed a projectile lodged in the lumbosacral canal. Surgical removal of the projectile was opted for, and during the procedure, the projectile was found to be intradural, necessitating a durotomy for extraction. Results: The uniqueness of each case encountered in the emergency room presents a challenging decision-making process. As Bono et.al. found, anatomical considerations, such as proximity to critical structures, as well as biomechanical stability, play a crucial role in treatment decisions. The most effective strategy remains prevention and the implementation of public policies aimed at disarming the population and promoting peace in cities. We believe that atypical cases should be discussed with patients and their families whenever possible. Conclusion: This study underscores the complexity of managing spinal firearm injuries, with each case requiring a tailored approach and careful evaluation of various clinical and ethical factors. It also highlights the importance of preventive measures and open communication with patients and their families.

## P633: Management of thoracolumbar transdiscal fractures complicating ankylosing spondylitis: a case series

Ben Mohamed Oussema

1

, Meddeb Mehdi

1

, Saadi Chedi

1

, Habboubi Khalil

1

, Mestiri Mondher

1

1

Institut Mohamed Kassab, Service Adulte, Tunis, Tunisia

Introduction: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is an inflammatory chronic rheumatic disease, which, if not treated appropriately, exposes the formation of the ankylosed or bamboo spine. The ankylosed spine is very susceptible to fracture. The aim of our work is to report on our experience in the management of AS patients with thoracolumbar fractures and their evolution. Material and Methods: This was a retrospective, descriptive study including patients followed for AS and managed for thoracolumbar transdiscal fractures in our institute, over a 14-year period. Patient data included age, sex, spinal fractures, clinical examination and paraclinical investigations. Therapeutic modalities and their evolution have also been reported. Results: Six patients with the mean age of 4 men and 2 women was 57.1 years were managed in our department. The average duration of AS was 13.8 years. The average follow-up in our study was 6.1 years. In most cases, the reason for hospitalization was trauma, most often minor. The mean time to fracture diagnosis was 19.4 weeks. Two patients with thoracic fractures had preoperative neurological complications. Non-surgical treatment was indicated for 3 patients for various reasons. Surgical treatment was indicated for 3 patients. Four patients had a favorable outcome. A was complicated by sepsis on the material followed by septic shock and death and another patient was complicated by kyphosis consolidation. Discussion: Trans-discal fractures results from fracture of the completely ankylosed spine. The mechanical stresses of this rigid spine prevent consolidation, leading to pseudarthrosis. These fractures were diagnosed on conventional radiography, CT and MRI. The management of transdiscal fractures in patients with AS is controversial, and there is no consensus on management. Non-operative management has a place in the therapeutic arsenal. Surgery is reserved for treatment in patients with deficit and dislocation or three-column injuries. circumferential arthrodesis with posterior instrumentation is considered the principal management. Conclusion: Spinal transdiscal fractures in patients with ankylosing spondylitis remain a rare and serious complication, exposing them to neurological complications. The mechanical nature of the pain and the notion of trauma, even minor, should prompt consideration of this diagnosis. The proposed treatment will depend on the medical and surgical findings.

Keywords: osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures; percutaneous stabilization;Short segment stablization; vertebroplasty.

## P636: Burst fracture of the thoracolumbar spine treat with Schanz screwes - 20 years of experience in a trauma hospital

Luan Rocha

Complexo Hospitalar do Trabalhador, Curitiba, Paraná, Brazil, Spine Surgery, Curitiba, Brazil

Introduction: The annual incidence of thoracolumbar fractures is about 30 individuals per 100,000 inhabitants, including osteoporotic fractures. In developing countries, the young population is more affected. Burst-type fractures involve anterior compression mechanisms and the involvement of the middle column, which can result in posterior fragments entering the vertebral canal. 90% of spinal fractures occur in the thoracolumbar segment. Schanz screw fixation allows effective distraction through the reduction maneuver by ligamentotaxis. Its use enables shorter surgical time, less bleeding, and satisfactory outcomes in restoring vertebral body height and reducing the Cobb angle postoperatively, with improved sagittal alignment. The objective of this study is to evaluate the experience with the use of Schanz screws in the treatment of AO type A3 and A4 burst fractures over 20 years. Evaluating a long period of technique use offers greater credibility in its application and clarifies the advantages, disadvantages, risks, and benefits of its use. The variables analyzed are: age, gender, type of fracture, affected spinal segment, need for material removal, time, and existing complications. SPSS 21 software was used. Results: A total of 313 cases were obtained, with the majority being male (74.9%). The thoracolumbar transition accounted for 227 cases. Correlating A3 and A4 fracture types with complications and hardware removal, we obtained p-values of 0.341 and 0.278, respectively, with A3 fractures presenting the highest number of complications. Conclusion: Burst fractures of the thoracolumbar transition, type A3 and A4, evaluated over 20 years and treated with Schanz screws, showed low complication rates with the use of the technique and a small need for hardware removal. The technique offers shorter, less invasive surgeries with good resolution.

Mohamed Ali

Objective: Although vertical laminar fracture (VLF) is generally considered a severity marker for thoracolumbar fractures (TLFs), its exact role in decision-making has never been established. Results: Twenty-eight studies were included in this systematic review, encompassing 2,021 patients, and twelve were included in the meta-analysis. According to the main subject of the study, the association of VLF with a dural laceration (n = 14), neurological deficit (n = 4), radiographic parameters (n = 3), thoracolumbar fracture classification (n = 2), treatment outcome (n = 2). The pooled OR estimates for VLF predicting dural lacerations was 7.75, 95% CI [2.41, 24.87]; p < 0.001). VLF may help preoperatively predict the risk of dural laceration, thereby choosing the optimal surgical strategy. Clinical and biomechanical data suggest VLF may be a valuable modifier to guide the decision-making in burst fractures; however, more studies are needed to confirm its prognostic importance regarding treatment outcomes.

## P638: How reliable is the distinction between thoracolumbar A3 and A4 fractures? Systematic literature review

Mohamed Ali

1

1

Prince Mohamed Ben Abdelaziz Hospital, Neurosurgery, NA, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

Study Design: systematic literature review. Objective: The AOSpine classification has classified thoracolumbar burst fractures into A3 and A4 fractures; however, previous studies reported fair to moderate interobserver reliability in diagnosing A3 and A4 fractures. The study aims to systematically analyze studies reporting the reliability of distinguishing between A3 and A4 fractures. Methods: We searched the PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for all studies reporting the inter- and intra-observer reliability on detecting thoracolumbar AO A3 and A4 fractures using computed tomography (CT). The search spanned 2013-2023 and included both reliability studies and interventional studies. Extracted data included author, year, design, sampling, patient and observer details, review specifics, study aims, and reliability findings. We followed the PRISMA guidelines and assessed the quality of the study using the modified COSMIN checklist. Kappa coefficient values were categorized according to Landis and Koch; from slight to excellent. Results: Of 396 identified studies, nine studies met the inclusion /exclusion criteria; all were reliability studies. Interobserver kappa values varied widely among studies, ranging from slight to almost perfect agreement (0.19 to 86). The interobserver reliability was poor in two studies, fair in one study, substantial in four studies, and excellent in one study. Only two studies reported intra-observer reliability, showing fair agreement (n = 1), or excellent agreement (n = 1). The included studies revealed significant heterogeneity in study design, sample size, and interpretation methods. Conclusion: Considerable variability exists in interobserver reliability for distinguishing A3 and A4 fractures. this variability might be attributed to methodological heterogeneity among studies, limitations of reliability analysis, or diagnostic pitfalls in differentiating between A3 and A4 fractures. More attention is needed during CT image interpretation to improve the accuracy in differentiation A3 and A4 fractures. Keywords: Thoracolumbar fractures, AOSpine classification, burst fractures, interobserver reliability, systematic review.

## P640: Corpectomies of the lower lumbar vertebral bodies (L4 and L5): single center experience, analysis of the postoperative results

Centre Hospitalier de Luxembourg, Luxembourg, Luxembourg

Introduction: This retrospective analysis aims to evaluate the surgical outcomes and complications associated with L4 and L5 corpectomies performed to treat vertebral fractures. One patient developed a postoperative infection requiring debridement and extended antibiotic therapy, while 2 patients experienced hardware failure, necessitating revision surgery. Adjacent segment degeneration occurred in 1 patient within 18 months of the procedure, managed conservatively. Conclusion: L4 and L5 corpectomies can provide substantial benefits in terms of pain relief, neurological recovery, and spinal stabilization for patients with severe vertebral fractures. However, the procedure carries a notable risk of complications, particularly hardware failure and postoperative infection. Careful surgical planning and postoperative management are essential to minimize these risks and optimize outcomes. Further studies with larger patient cohorts are needed to better define the long-term efficacy and complication rates of L4 and L5 corpectomies.

## P641: The use of transpedicular Schanz screws on AO B2 fractures of the spine: a novel approach on the matter

Guilherme Laffitte

, Luan Rocha

, Álynson Larocca Kulcheski

1

, André Luís Sebben

, Pedro Grein

, Felipe Nanni

, Joao Elias

, Xavier Soler I Graells

1

1

Complexo Hospital do Trabalhador, Ortopedia e Traumatologia - Coluna, Curitiba, Brazil

Introduction: The hyperflexion fracture of the spine with lesion to the posterior tension band has always been deemed as a surgical fracture, unless the patient was unfit for surgery. Although this remains true, the technique that should be used for these types of fracture are still varied and no consensus has been achieved. Several Trauma Centres have been using mostly pedicle screws for these fractures, aiming for an effective arthrodesis of the affected level and secondary stabilization of the fracture. On more recent articles review, the fracture fixation technique with transpedicular Schanz screws are being used in place of the complete arthrodesis with pedicle screws successfully, being able to maintain a good stabilization of the fracture and achieving bone healing with a less expensive and less traumatic technique. This result is counterintuitive given the supposed nature of these types of fractures. Only 4 patients had complications, 3 reoperations for removal of the construct and one surgical site infection. The effectiveness of the overall treatment was comparable to the ones where pedicle screws were used. Conclusion: Patients with B2 hyperflexions type fractures are typically indicated to do pedicle screws arthrodesis. As it has been shown in this study, the use of Schanz construct can yield good results for these types of lesions, with relatively low rate of complications and a very high surgeon and patient satisfaction post operatively. Therefore more research and clinical trials should be performed to further evaluate and establish the use and effectiveness of this technique as another possible indication for this type of fracture.

## P642: Evaluation of loss of correction in percutaneous versus open surgery for type A thoracolumbar spine fracture: a comparative study

Sami Bahroun

1

, Anis Bouaziz

, Mohamed Samih Kacem

1

, Ameur Triki

1

, Masmoudi Zied

1

, Mohamed Samir Daghfous

1

1

Kassab Hspital, Orthopaedic Department B, Tunis, Tunisia

Background: The management of type A thoracolumbar fractures can be approached through either percutaneous or open surgery techniques. This study aims to compare the radiological outcomes of these two methods in the treatment of type A compression fractures. Materials and Methods: This retrospective comparative cohort study included patients who underwent surgery for thoracolumbar type A fractures, either through a percutaneous or open surgical approach. Inclusion criteria were type A1 and A2 compression fractures, while type A3 burst fractures or fractures associated with neurological deficits were excluded. The Cobb angle and Traumatic Regional Angulation (TRA) were measured preoperatively, immediately postoperatively, and at the last follow-up for both groups. ## P643: Open versus percutaneous fixation of thoracolumbar burst fractures - Comparison of pain and mobility related outcomes

Srivathsan Ramesh

1

, Nikhil Gattu

1

, Jackson Burns

1

, Maile Curbo

1

, Jacob Siahaan

1

, James Showery

1

1

McGovern Medical School, Houston, United States

Introduction: Percutaneous and open fixation are two widely accepted forms of fixation for the treatment of thoracolumbar burst fractures. In previous studies, both forms of fixation have been proven to have acceptable outcomes both radiologically and clinically. To our knowledge, there are currently no studies examining postoperative pain and mobility differences in these two cohorts. Therefore, the aim of this study was to compare pain medication requirements and mobility differences between patients who receive open fixation and percutaneous fixation for thoracolumbar burst fractures. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective chart review of patients with thoracolumbar burst fractures treated with percutaneous stabilization or open fixation at a single institution. We queried our electronic medical record utilizing CPT codes (22325, 22327). Inclusion criteria consisted of patients between 17-65 years old, AO B2, A3, or A4 fractures with or without PLC disruption, and fractures at the levels of T10-L2. Exclusion criteria consisted of polytrauma, neurological deficits, injuries precluding ambulation status, pathologic fractures, delayed presentation > 1 week after injury, extension type injuries, Charcot spine, revision cases, and degenerative cases. For each patient, we recorded preoperative, postoperative day 1, and discharge AMPAC scores to assess mobility, preoperative, postoperative day 1, 2, and 3 morphine milligram equivalent (MME) requirements, preoperative and postoperative Sagittal Cobb angles, length of hospital stay, radiation/fluoroscopy dose, blood loss, discharge disposition, operative time, number of levels fused, and posterior ligamentous complex (PLC) injury. Continuous variables were analyzed with Mann Whitney U-Tests. Chi-squared tests were utilized for categorical variables. Statistical significance was indicated as p-value less than 0.05. Results: 17 patients were included in the percutaneous fixation group and 63 patients were included in the open fixation group. The average age of patients in the percutaneous cohort was 41.2 ± 13.0 compared to 38.3 ± 12.9 in the open cohort. There was a significant difference (p < 0.001) between the radiation exposure for percutaneous (98.9 gy ± 63.6) and open (24 gy ± 27.2) groups. Additionally, there was a significant difference (p < 0.001) in the average EBL of percutaneous (49.1 mL ± 43.6) versus open (271 mL ± 320.4) groups. There was also a significant difference in operative time between the open (3.0 hours) and percutaneous (2.3) hours (p < 0.01) without a significant difference in fused levels. In a sub-group analysis of the percutaneous group there was a significant difference between the amount of radiation in navigation (143.5 gy ± 56.2) versus non navigation (60.6 ± 42) groups. There were no statistical differences between groups for mobility, pain medications, cobb angles, hospital stay, number of levels fused, need for blood transfusion, discharge disposition or adverse outcomes. Conclusion: Percutaneous fixation for thoracolumbar injuries is associated with higher doses of radiation and lower surgeon estimated blood loss as compared to open fixation. Along with that, open fixation of these injuries had a significantly longer operative time than percutaneous fixation and were predominantly used when there were associated PLC injuries. However, there were no statistically significant differences between the two surgical modalities in terms of post operative mobility or pain medication requirements.

## P644: Thoracolumbar spinal injuries in surfing: a systematic review

Ella Sanford

1

, Sahil Garg

2

, Kyle Jamar

3

, Sonny Gill

4

, Michael Gallizzi

4

1
Colorado State University, Fort Collins, United States,

2
Steadman Philippon Research Institute, Center for Outcomes Based Orthopaedic Research, Spine Research, Vail, United States,

3
University of Colorado School of Medicine, Aurora, United States,

4

The Steadman Clinic, Spine Surgery, Vail, United States

Introduction: As surfing has gained popularity and recognition, even making its Olympic debut in the 2020 Games, the risks associated with the sport have become more apparent. Among these, spinal injuries, though rare, can be particularly debilitating. Existing literature highlights that spinal injuries are the leading musculoskeletal injuries suffered by surfers. Despite this, little is known about epidemiology surrounding the etiology of spinal injury. This review discusses the types of injuries commonly associated with surfing, as well as strategies for management and prevention that are essential for healthcare professionals involved in treating surfers. The goal is to assess the incidence, prevalence, diagnostic methods, management strategies, and outcomes of these injuries in surfers. By synthesizing existing research, the paper aims to provide insights into the patterns of injury, identify gaps in the literature, and offer recommendations for the prevention and treatment of thoracolumbar spine injuries in the surfing population. Material and Methods: This systematic review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The search strategy involved a comprehensive search of PubMed and Google Scholar up to November 2023, using MeSH terms and simple search methods to gather relevant articles. Studies included in the review reported on both acute and chronic thoracolumbar spine injuries in the context of surfing. Two independent reviewers screened the titles and abstracts of identified studies for eligibility. The included studies comprised primary research and systematic reviews reporting thoracolumbar injuries. Measures were taken to avoid duplicate case reporting by reviewing the sources of cases in systematic reviews. Results: A total of 43 studies were included in the final review. 949 individual injuries were identified. 25% (n = 241) of injuries were due to a sprain, strain, or contusion. 10% (n = 95) of injuries were due to Surfer’s Myelopathy. 3% (27) of the injuries were fractures. 62% (n = 586) of reported thoracolumbar injuries had an unspecified diagnosis. Conclusion: Commonly reported injuries in the thoracolumbar spine sustained as a result of surfing include surfer's myelopathy, strains, sprains, and contusions. While less frequent, it is essential to consider higher-energy injuries such as vertebral column fractures during the initial evaluation of a patient. Improving core strength, balance, and coordination has been shown to be effective in the prevention and treatment of common injuries. Placing clinical emphasis on these aspects of physical fitness can contribute significantly to both treatment and injury prevention among surfers.

## P645: Seated facet block for the treatment of osteoporotic vertebral fractures in the context of respiratory contraindications: a case report

Carlos Betancourt Quiroz

1

, Eduardo Callejas

1

, Jose Carlos Sauri Barraza

1

1

Centro Médico ABC Santa Fe, Cirugía de Columna Vertebral, Ciudad de México

Introduction: Osteoporotic vertebral fractures are a common occurrence in elderly populations, often leading to chronic pain, disability, and decreased quality of life. Standard treatments like vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty, while effective for pain relief and mechanical stabilization, pose significant risks in patients with comorbidities such as pulmonary or cardiovascular conditions. In patients with severe respiratory insufficiency, these procedures can exacerbate respiratory dysfunction, necessitating the exploration of less invasive alternatives. This case report highlights the successful use of a seated facet block in a patient with multiple osteoporotic fractures and severe respiratory contraindications. Material and Methods: A 70-year-old female patient with a history of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and chronic respiratory insufficiency presented with intense thoracolumbar pain that significantly limited her mobility and worsened her respiratory symptoms. Imaging studies revealed recent osteoporotic compression fractures at T10, L1, and L4. Due to the patient’s severe respiratory dysfunction, vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty were contraindicated, and an alternative approach was required to manage her pain while minimizing procedural risks. A seated facet block was chosen as the therapeutic option to address her pain without exacerbating her pulmonary condition. The procedure was performed under fluoroscopic guidance using the Philips Allura Xper FD20 system. The patient was seated to avoid the prone position, which could have compromised her respiratory function. A total of 10 mL of medication per treated level was administered, consisting of 1 mL of methylprednisolone (40 mg/mL), 9 mL of ropivacaine (2 mg/mL), and 1 mL of non-ionic contrast medium (370 mg iodine/mL). The injection targeted the medial branches of the affected vertebral levels (T10, L1, L4) to provide both immediate pain relief and a long-lasting anti-inflammatory effect. Results: The patient experienced a marked reduction in pain, with her Visual Analog Scale (VAS) score decreasing from 8/10 pre-procedure to 1/10 immediately after the facet block. The procedure was well-tolerated, with no respiratory complications observed during or after the intervention. Follow-up evaluations at one week, one month, and three months post-procedure revealed sustained pain relief, improved mobility, and an overall enhancement in her quality of life. Additionally, the patient reported improved breathing as a result of reduced thoracolumbar pain, which had previously restricted her respiratory function. Conclusion: The seated facet block was a safe and effective option for managing osteoporotic vertebral fractures in a patient with severe respiratory comorbidities. This technique allowed for significant pain relief without the risks associated with more invasive procedures such as vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty. The use of a seated position, combined with fluoroscopic guidance and a local anesthetic-corticosteroid mixture, provided both immediate and long-term benefits. This case highlights the importance of individualized treatment approaches in patients with significant comorbidities and supports the use of seated facet blocks as a viable alternative in managing complex cases of osteoporotic vertebral fractures where standard treatments are contraindicated. Further studies are warranted to establish this technique as a standard option for patients with similar profiles.

## P646: Machine learning models for predicting surgical complications in thoracolumbar spine trauma

Charles Carazzo

1

, Guillermo Ricciardi

2

, Ratko Yurac

3

, Alfredo Guiroy

4

, Juan P. Cabrera

5

, Joana Guasque

6

, Asdrubal Falavigna

7

1
São Vicente de Paulo Hospital, Neurosurgery, Passo Fundo, Brazil,

2
Centro Médico Integral Fitz Roy, Orthopaedics and Traumatology, Buenos Aires, Argentina,

3
Universidad del Desarrollo, Department of Orthopedic and Traumatology, Santiago, Chile,

4
Elite Spine Health and Wellness Center, Florida, United States,

5
Hospital Clínico Regional de Concepción, Department of Neurosurgery, Concepción, Chile,

6
Cajuru University Hospital, Orthopaedics and Traumatology, Curitiba, Brazil,

7

Caxias do Sul University, Neurosurgery, Caxias do Sul, Brazil

Introduction: Unstable traumatic thoracolumbar fractures, often resulting from high-energy trauma, present a complex clinical scenario with variable outcomes influenced by factors such as timing of surgical intervention and risk of complications. Accurate prediction of post-operative complications could significantly enhance treatment decisions in these cases, prompting exploration into the potential of machine learning, particularly in predictive modeling within medicine. This paper provides a detailed investigation into the development and validation of machine learning models for predicting surgical complications in thoracolumbar spine trauma. Material and Methods: Clinical data from 525 patients across 21 spine centers in nine Latin American countries were retrospectively collected, with “Complications” serving as the binary target variable indicating postoperative complications. Preprocessing ensured data quality and compatibility with machine learning algorithms. Multiple machine learning models, including Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and XGBoost, were evaluated for their predictive performance. Additionally, a deep learning model was developed using a sequential architecture. Models were trained and assessed based on various metrics such as Accuracy, F1 Score, Recall, Precision, and AUC. Results: Five machine learning models were evaluated on a classification task. In the Logistic Regression model, an accuracy of approximately 74.29% was exhibited. The F1 Score was 0.81. The AUC was 0.60, which is relatively low. The Decision Tree model had an accuracy of approximately 70.48%, with an F1 Score of 0.79. It achieved the highest Recall among all the models (0.86), indicating the highest proportion of true positives identified. However, its Precision of 0.74 is lower than that of Logistic Regression, indicating a higher proportion of false positives. Random Forest presented a slightly lower accuracy than the Decision Tree, at approximately 69.52%. The F1 Score was 0.79 and the Recall was the highest among the models (0.87), indicating a strong ability to identify the positive class. Nevertheless, it had the lowest Precision (0.72), and the AUC of 0.73 indicates a differentiation capacity similar to that of the Decision Tree. The SVM model showed the lowest accuracy (68.57%) among the evaluated models. Despite this, it had a competitive F1 Score of 0.79 and the highest Recall (0.91), indicating a tendency to predict the positive class, but with the lowest Precision (0.70), resulting in more false positives. The XGBoost model achieved the highest accuracy (73.33%) and an F1 Score of 0.81, showing a good balance between Recall (0.88) and Precision (0.75). However, the AUC was 0.64, the second-lowest among the models, suggesting that while the model is accurate, its capability to separate the classes is not ideal. Conclusion: In conclusion, while different models exhibit varying strengths and weaknesses, XGBoost appears to be the most promising model for this classification task due to its high accuracy and balanced F1 Score. However, further optimization may be necessary to improve the model's ability to differentiate between classes, as indicated by its relatively low AUC. Additionally, the choice of model should consider the specific requirements of the classification task, such as the importance of minimizing false positives or false negatives.

## P647: Injury profile and neurological outcomes of high energy thoracic spine fractures after surgery and middle term follow-up

Marcel Castelo

1,2

, Johan Hurtado

1

1
Hospital Antonio Lorena, Department of Neurosurgery, Cusco, Peru,

2

Universidad Nacional San Antonio Abad del Cusco, Cusco, Peru

Objective: Morphological and neurological features of thoracic spine fractures, in close relation to the spinal cord and thorax, set them apart from the rest of spine. This segment has special biomechanic behavior and the whole spectrum of their traumatic injuries has not been fully described in the middle or long-term follow-up after surgery. The aim of this retrospective study was to correlate the spine and spinal cord injury pattern of high energy thoracic fractures with their outcomes in a surgically treated patient cohort. Materials and Methods: We studied the baseline profile of 73 patients admitted to our hospital with thoracic spine fractures between 2016 and 2023, reviewing their clinical profile, spine injury type and AO classification, surgical strategies, general and surgical complications, and outcomes during an 18 month mean follow-up period. Statistical analysis of possible associations between variables was carried out. Results: Motor vehicle accident was the main injury mechanism. 75% had thoracic complications such as hemothorax or cardiovascular instability, and 48% were tributary of intensive care management at the ICU. 65% of patients (47/73) had a variable spectrum of neurological deficit, mainly complete SCI (ASIA A); meanwhile 50% of those with neurological impairment presented general complications (p = 0.003) before surgery and delayed the procedure. Most of cases underwent a multilevel posterior arthrodesis, average 4.6 vertebrae, and short instrumentations were not used at all. Surgical complications were related to hemothorax increase, acute anemia and thrombosis in 20% of cases. 15% of patients needed surgical revision and reposition of screws due to misplacement. In the follow-up view, neurological status improved ≥ 1 ASIA level in 42% of incomplete SCI and in 18% of complete SCI after 6 months, and it raised to 21% at 12 months (in the field of intensive physiotherapy). Full dependence rate was 92% at discharge, reduced to 88% at 6 months and 77% at 12 months. A mean value of 8.2° loss correction was observed in the whole cohort at 6 months of radiological control, and bone fusion was observed at an average of 10.3 ± 3.8 months, with 81% of pedicle screws considered stable. Autonomic disfunction were not routine evaluated. In-patient mortality was 2.73% (2/73 patients), and it raised to 5.1% at 12 months. Conclusion: High energy thoracic spine fractures have a very high complications and neurological disability rate, even after ICU support and a prompt neurosurgical management. Fast decompression, extensive fixation and strong fusion were related, but not statistically associated, to neurological improvement and a better biomechanical correction and fusion in these cohort. A prolonged follow-up of patients as well as autonomic disability evaluation is mandatory to understand the real scope of changes in this type of injuries in prospective series.

## P649: Percutaneous fixation vs. conservative treatment in osteoporotic vertebral fractures: a comparative study on regional kyphosis correction

Victor Martin-Gorgojo

1,2

, Antonio Silvestre Muñoz

2,3,4

, Sonia Muñoz Donat

4

, Sara Burguet Girona

5

, Miguel Tena Roig

4

, José Miguel Molina Márquez

4

, Antonio Martín-Benlloch

3 6

1
NSW Spine Specialists, Sydney, Australia,

2
Biomedical Research Institute INCLIVA, Clinic University Hospital, Valencia, Spain,

3
University of Valencia, Department of Surgery (Orthopedics), Valencia, Spain,

4
Clinic University Hospital of Valencia, Orthopedic Surgery and Traumatology Department, Valencia, Spain,

5
Hospital IMED Colón, Valencia, Spain,

6

Dr. Peset University Hospital, Orthopedic Surgery and Traumatology Department, Valencia, Spain

Introduction: Osteoporotic vertebral fractures (OVFs) are becoming more common due to the increasing incidence of osteoporosis in aging populations. Despite advances in treatment, the optimal approach for managing OVFs remains unclear due to limited evidence and lack of international consensus. This study aimed to compare the effectiveness of percutaneous fixation (PF) vs conservative treatment in correcting regional kyphosis in patients with acute OVFs. Materials and Methods: Retrospective analytical study including patients admitted to a tertiary hospital with single-level OVF at the thoracolumbar junction (T10-L2), classified as AO-Spine DGOU OF3 or OF4, confirmed by CT and MRI. Patients were treated either conservatively with a thoracolumbar brace or surgically with short or long PF, without screw augmentation or cementing techniques. Based on sample size calculations, 21 patients per group were included. Radiological follow-up was performed at 4-6 weeks and 3-6 months post-fracture. Statistical analysis included bivariate tests and covariance analysis with bootstrap resampling to control for covariates, with a p-value of < 0.05 considered significant. The study period spanned from May 31, 2020, to March 31, 2023. Results: A total of 42 patients were included, with 21 in each group. The conservative group was older (82.0 [78.0-86.0] vs. 79.5 [73.0-82.3] years, p < 0.001) and had higher Charlson comorbidity index scores (4.9 ± 1.6 points vs. 3.4 ± 1.3 points, p = 0.005). No significant differences were found between the groups in fracture level or subtype based on AO-Spine DGOU or Genant classifications. At baseline, the conservative group had lower Hounsfield unit scores on CT (67.0 ± 20.9 HU vs. 95.2 ± 31.0 HU, p = 0.001) and slightly higher pelvic incidence (56.3 ± 9.8º vs. 50.5 ± 8.1º, p = 0.042). In terms of regional kyphosis correction, the PF group showed a 25.5% improvement at 4–6 weeks, but this regressed by 35.0% at 3–6 months, resulting in a net change of only 0.1%. The conservative group experienced a 61.6% deterioration in the first 4–6 weeks, followed by an additional 3.4% decline. Final regional kyphosis progression was significantly greater in the brace group (+6.2 ± 5.4º vs. +0.1 ± 8.1º, p = 0.007). Age and Charlson comorbidity index were significantly correlated with regional kyphosis correction (p = 0.015 and p = 0.014, respectively). However, after adjusting for these factors, no significant differences in regional kyphosis correction were found between the treatment groups (p = 0.139). Additionally, the conservative group showed a compensatory increase in lumbar lordosis (57.1 ± 14.2º vs. 46.1 ± 12.0º, p = 0.010) and reduced thoraco-lumbar kyphosis (19.2 ± 13.6 vs. 24.4 ± 12.9º, p = 0.043), leading to no significant differences in sagittal spinal alignment (sagittal vertical axis, pelvic incidence-lumbar lordosis mismatch, or global tilt). Conclusion: Percutaneous fixation for OVFs did not show superiority over conservative treatment in correcting the regional kyphosis angle. Conservative treatment should still be considered a viable option for managing acute OVFs, particularly in patients with higher comorbidities, reducing the risks associated with surgery.

Adjacent vertebral fractures occurred in 10 cases (19.2%). Preexisting vertebral fractures occurred in 29 cases (55.8%), and preexisting disease was present in 14 cases (26.9%). There were no postoperative complications. There were no differences in the mechanism of injury, adjacent vertebral fractures, pre-existing conditions, or postoperative complications in the 85-plus age group compared to the 80-84 age group. Conclusion: VBS had a stable outcome in the elderly over 80 years of age. The same was true for very elderly patients aged 85 years or older. The complications were also low, and VBS was considered to be a worthwhile procedure for elderly patients.

## P651: Low-cost minimally invasive surgery lumbar spine bullet fragment removal: 10 cases reports

Francisco Moura Neto

Orizonti Institute, Belo Horizonte, Brazil

Introduction: Treatment of gunshot wounds to the spine is a topic of continued discussion and controversy. Material and Methods: Immediately after the gunshot wound, the patient developed low back pain, radicular or neurological deficits. The patients who remained with the bullet in the canal were taken for surgery to remove the retained bullet, using a tubular system made with syringes in varying sizes. Results: Following surgery, pain and neurologic function improved. The operative technique and the postoperative clinical showed that a minimally invasive approach made it possible to perform a safe and effective surgery, with a reduction in surgical time and clinical improvement. Conclusion: In our opinion, it was necessary to remove the projectile to prevent migration and possible worsening of neurological function. However, surgical intervention is not appropriate in all cases and, ultimately, decisions should be based on the patient's presentation, symptomatology and imaging tests.

## P652: AO Spine Thoracolumbar Burst Fractures Type A3 and A4 - Characterizing patients with very poor performance after treatment

Jonathan Dalton

1

, Rajkishen Narayanan
